Introduction Arthropod-borne viruses (arboviruses), particularly those transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, constitute an increasing public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa. Among these diseases, dengue is the most prevalent and poses the greatest public health burden, with more than half of the global population at risk and an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring annually [1]. In Burkina Faso, the epidemiology of dengue has changed markedly over the past decade, with successive outbreaks reported in 2016, 2017, and, most notably, in 2023, when the country experienced its largest documented epidemic [2–4]. Recent entomological investigations have identified Aedes aegypti as the principal vector responsible for dengue transmission in the country [5, 6] . Aedes aegypti is a highly anthropophilic mosquito that has successfully adapted to human-modified environments, enabling its persistence and expansion in rapidly urbanizing areas[7]. The abundance and distribution of this mosquito are governed by the interaction between climatic conditions and anthropogenic environmental changes. Rainfall directly influences the availability of breeding habitats by creating both natural and artificial water-holding containers, thereby promoting immature mosquito development [8, 9]. However, anthropogenic activities substantially amplify these effects by increasing the number and diversity of artificial larval habitats. Discarded tires, water storage jars and barrels, plastic containers, metal cans, construction debris and abandoned vehicles provide highly productive breeding sites that can sustain Ae. aegypti populations even during prolonged dry periods, when natural aquatic habitats become scarce [7, 10, 11]. In addition, household practices such as domestic water storage, inadequate solid waste management and poor environmental sanitation further enhance larval habitat availability and contribute to persistent vector proliferation. Page 3/19 Bobo-Dioulasso, the second largest city in Burkina Faso provides an ideal setting for investigating the interactions between climatic and anthropogenic drivers of Ae. aegypti abundance. Located within the Sudanian climatic zone, the city comprises densely populated urban neighborhoods surrounded by peri-urban and rural communities, creating a pronounced gradient of environmental conditions human activities, and infrastructure [12, 13]. Urban neighborhoods are characterized by high human population density, irregular water supply, widespread domestic water storage and inadequate solid waste management, all of which generate abundant and persistent breeding habitats for Ae. Aegypti [6, 12, 14, 15]. Conversely, rural areas are more strongly influenced by seasonal rainfall which creates transient breeding sites such as tree holes and temporary pools while household water storage practices allow vector populations to persist throughout the dry season [16]. Although rainfall and anthropogenic factors are widely recognized as key determinants of Ae. aegypti ecology, their combined influence on mosquito abundance has received limited attention in Burkina Faso, particularly across urban-rural gradients. Most previous studies have focused either on seasonal variation of vector populations or upon characterization of breeding habitats without explicitly quantifying the interactive effects of climatic and human-related factors on larval density. Addressing this knowledge gap is essential for developing integrated and context-specific vector control strategies that incorporate both environmental variability and human behavioral determinants [17]. In this study, we investigated the combined effects of rainfall and anthropogenic activities on Aedes aegypti density across urban and rural settings in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. Specifically, we quantified larval density and standard entomological indices during the dry and rainy seasons and assessed the influence of climatic variables and container characteristics on larval abundance. Our findings provide evidence to support targeted, context-specific vector control interventions in areas at high risk of arboviral transmission. Materials and Methods Study area The study was conducted in Bobo-Dioulasso (11°11′N, 4°17′W), the second largest city in Burkina Faso, located at Guiriko Region in the southwestern part of the country (Figure 1). The city lies within the Sudanian climatic zone, which is characterized by two distinct seasons: a rainy season extending from May to October and a dry season from November to April. Annual rainfall ranges between 900 and 1,200 mm, while mean annual temperatures vary from 25°C to 32°C. This climatic regime provides favorable conditions for the seasonal development of Aedes aegypti populations. Two study sites with contrasting ecological and socio-environmental characteristics were selected to represent urban and rural settings within the city: Sector 6 (urban) and Sector 33 (rural) (Figure 1). Selection and description of study sites Urban site (Sector 6) Sector 6 was selected to represent the urban setting because of its position, planned residential layout, and relatively well- developed urban infrastructure. According to the RGPH 2019, sector 6 has a population of 12,266 and comprises 2,926 households. The area is characterized by paved roads, a formal drainage network for wastewater and stormwater, and access to piped water, electricity, health facilities, schools and municipal waste collection services. Housing is predominantly constructed with cement blocks and arranged in planned residential plots. Despite these urban amenities, numerous artificial water-holding containers capable of supporting Ae. aegypti breeding were observed around households including discarded tires, plastic containers, flower pots, blocked drains and domestic water-storage containers. These breeding habitats are largely associated with human activities and urban waste accumulation. Page 4/19 Rural site (Sector 33) Although administratively part of the city of Bobo‐Dioulasso, sector 33 displays ecological and socio‐economic characteristics typical of rural settings (limited infrastructure, reliance on water storage, and proximity to vegetated areas). For this reason, we refer to it as a rural site in the present study. According to the RGPH 2019, sector 33 has a population of 27,251 and comprises 5,956 households. Most houses are constructed from traditional materials (banco or adobe) and potential mosquito breeding habitats consisted of both natural and artificial water-holding sites, including three holes, leaf axils temporary rain-filled puddles, watering troughs, buckets and domestic water-storage containers. Compared with the urban site, aquatic habitats were generally more dispersed and frequently associated with agricultural and household activities. Rationale for site selection The two study sites were selected to capture the environmental and anthropogenic heterogeneity that characterizes Bobo-Dioulasso. Sector 6 represents a highly urbanized environment where vector breeding is primarily associated with artificial containers generated by human activities, intensive urbanization, and high population density. Conversely, Sector 33 represents a predominantly rural environment, where mosquito breeding habitats arise from a combination of natural water collections and domestic water-storage practices under conditions of limited infrastructure. Comparing these contrasting settings provides an opportunity to evaluate how rainfall, sanitation infrastructure, waste management, housing characteristics and water-storage practices influence Aedes aegypti larval abundance under different ecological and socio-economic conditions within the same metropolitan area (Figure 2). This urban-rural comparison also enables the identification of context-specific determinants of vector proliferation that may inform targeted surveillance and control strategies. Study design and data collection Prior to conducting the larval surveys, verbal informed consent was obtained from the head of each household. This study was conducted in two contrasting sites within Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso: Sector 6 (urban) and Sector 33 (rural). Entomological surveys were carried out during the dry season (February, April, and December 2025) and the rainy season (June, September, and October 2025). Thirty (30) households per site were visited during each survey campaign. During each survey, every water-holding container found within each visited concession was systematically inspected. All inspected containers were recorded using a tablet equipped with a standardized data collection form specifically designed for this study. For each container, the following data were recorded: sector, concession identifier, container type, presence or absence of water, presence or absence of larvae (including larval stage) or pupae, water source (rainwater, borehole water, or National Office for Water and Sanitation (ONEA) tap water), water clarity (clear, turbid, or purulent), and presence of vegetation around and inside the container. When larvae or pupae were present, they were collected using a pipette or dipper, transferred into a labelled container and transported to the laboratory. Upon arrival at the laboratory, each container was opened by number, emptied and treated to remove impurities. Larval identification was performed using standard morphological keys based on the respiratory siphon: Anopheles larvae lack a siphon, Aedes larvae possess a short siphon and Culex larvae possess a long siphon [18]. After identification, larvae were counted and the count was recorded directly into the tablet. These data were subsequently used to calculate larval density, entomological indices (Breteau Index, House Index, Container Index) [19] and the density of positive breeding sites per concession. Page 5/19 Data management and statistical analysis All field data were collected using standardized entomological survey forms and entered into a secure database (Microsoft Excel 2016). Three classical entomological indices were calculated to assess the level of Aedes aegypti infestation across sites and seasons: Breteau Index (BI): number of positive containers per 100 inspected premises. House Index (HI): percentage of premises positive for at least one container with Aedes larvae. Container Index (CI): percentage of water‐holding containers positive for Aedes larvae. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.3.2) [20], with the significance threshold set at α = 0.05. To evaluate the impact of rainfall and anthropogenic activities on larval density, a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a negative binomial distribution was fitted. Larval count was used as the response variable, while site (urban vs. rural), season, rainfall, temperature and humidity were included as fixed effects. Concession ID and collection date were treated as random effects to account for repeated measures. Pearson correlation analysis was conducted to explore relationships among environmental parameters and their association with larval abundance. Differences in mean larval densities across sites and seasons were tested using ANOVA, followed by Tukey’s post hoc comparisons when significant differences were detected. Results General description of sampling A total of 816 water-holding containers were inspected across the study area. The most frequently encountered container types were kettles (19.1%, 95% CI: 16.4-21.8), terracotta jars (18.4%, 95% CI: 15.8-21.1) and barrels (16.1%, 95% CI: 13.6- 18.6). Tires (12.0%, 95% CI: 9.8-14.3) and cans (10.7%, 95% CI: 8.6-12.9) also represented a substantial proportion of inspected containers, while watering holes (8.6%), buckets (4.3%), domestic materials (3.8%), flower pots (2.6%), basins (2.1%) and animal skins (0.2%) were less common. Positivity rates varied across container types: terracotta jars (18.0%), barrels (13.0%), tires (21.4%), cans (27.6%), watering holes (21.4%), buckets (22.9%), domestic materials (41.9%), flower pots (28.6%) and basins (29.4%) showed notable proportions of positive containers whereas kettles (5.8%) and animal skins (0%) had the lowest positivity. Page 2/19 Abstract Aedes aegypti, the primary vector of dengue, chikungunya and Zika, breeds mainly in artificial containers around households, and its larval abundance reflects a complex interplay between climate and human practices. In our cross- sectional survey conducted in urban and rural sectors of Bobo-Dioulasso across dry and rainy seasons, entomological indices exceeded WHO epidemic thresholds, with the House Index reaching 66.7% and the Breteau Index ranging from 107 to 147, indicating sustained transmission risk. Infestation varied markedly by container type. Domestic materials (41.9%), basins (29.4%) and flower pots (28.6%) showed the highest positivity rates, whereas kettles and animal skins were rarely colonized. Notably, although less frequent, terracotta jars, barrels, tires and miscellaneous containers produced more than 70% of all larvae, identifying them as principal production sites. This confirms that structural characteristics of containers, rather than their abundance alone, decisively shape larval habitat suitability. Seasonality also structured larval dynamics. More containers were positive during the dry season, but mean density was three-fold higher in the rainy season, with rainfall exhibiting a non-linear relationship, intermediate precipitation promoting proliferation. After accounting for climatic variables, urban households consistently harbored higher larval densities, reflecting intensive water storage and inadequate waste management. Collectively, proliferation is driven by the combined effects of rainfall dynamics and human practices. Container-related structural and ecological factors, type, exposure and organic matter, therefore exert a more pronounced influence on larval productivity than mere container availability. Interventions should prioritize highly productive containers, particularly jars, barrels and tires, by integrating rainfall-based surveillance with community-led source reduction in areas at greatest transmission risk. Introduction Arthropod-borne viruses (arboviruses), particularly those transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, constitute an increasing public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa. Among these diseases, dengue is the most prevalent and poses the greatest public health burden, with more than half of the global population at risk and an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring annually [1]. In Burkina Faso, the epidemiology of dengue has changed markedly over the past decade, with successive outbreaks reported in 2016, 2017, and, most notably, in 2023, when the country experienced its largest documented epidemic [2–4]. Recent entomological investigations have identified Aedes aegypti as the principal vector responsible for dengue transmission in the country [5, 6] . Aedes aegypti is a highly anthropophilic mosquito that has successfully adapted to human-modified environments, enabling its persistence and expansion in rapidly urbanizing areas[7]. The abundance and distribution of this mosquito are governed by the interaction between climatic conditions and anthropogenic environmental changes. Rainfall directly influences the availability of breeding habitats by creating both natural and artificial water-holding containers, thereby promoting immature mosquito development [8, 9]. However, anthropogenic activities substantially amplify these effects by increasing the number and diversity of artificial larval habitats. Discarded tires, water storage jars and barrels, plastic containers, metal cans, construction debris and abandoned vehicles provide highly productive breeding sites that can sustain Ae. aegypti populations even during prolonged dry periods, when natural aquatic habitats become scarce [7, 10, 11]. In addition, household practices such as domestic water storage, inadequate solid waste management and poor environmental sanitation further enhance larval habitat availability and contribute to persistent vector proliferation. Page 3/19 Bobo-Dioulasso, the second largest city in Burkina Faso provides an ideal setting for investigating the interactions between climatic and anthropogenic drivers of Ae. aegypti abundance. Located within the Sudanian climatic zone, the city comprises densely populated urban neighborhoods surrounded by peri-urban and rural communities, creating a pronounced gradient of environmental conditions human activities, and infrastructure [12, 13]. Urban neighborhoods are characterized by high human population density, irregular water supply, widespread domestic water storage and inadequate solid waste management, all of which generate abundant and persistent breeding habitats for Ae. Aegypti [6, 12, 14, 15]. Conversely, rural areas are more strongly influenced by seasonal rainfall which creates transient breeding sites such as tree holes and temporary pools while household water storage practices allow vector populations to persist throughout the dry season [16]. Although rainfall and anthropogenic factors are widely recognized as key determinants of Ae. aegypti ecology, their combined influence on mosquito abundance has received limited attention in Burkina Faso, particularly across urban-rural gradients. Most previous studies have focused either on seasonal variation of vector populations or upon characterization of breeding habitats without explicitly quantifying the interactive effects of climatic and human-related factors on larval density. Addressing this knowledge gap is essential for developing integrated and context-specific vector control strategies that incorporate both environmental variability and human behavioral determinants [17]. In this study, we investigated the combined effects of rainfall and anthropogenic activities on Aedes aegypti density across urban and rural settings in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. Specifically, we quantified larval density and standard entomological indices during the dry and rainy seasons and assessed the influence of climatic variables and container characteristics on larval abundance. Our findings provide evidence to support targeted, context-specific vector control interventions in areas at high risk of arboviral transmission. elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在了解布基纳法索西部博博迪乌拉索城乡环境中埃及伊蚊繁殖地感染和幼虫密度的驱动因素,因为这些蚊子是登革热、基孔肯雅热和寨卡病毒的主要 媒介。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 在旱季和雨季对博博迪乌拉索的城乡进行了横断面调查。昆虫学指数超过世卫组织流行阈值,House指数达到66.7%,Breteau指数在107至147之间,表明传播风险持续存在。
elements_zh.methods: 感染情况因容器类型而异,家用材料、盆和花盆的阳性率最高,而水壶和动物皮毛很少被感染。该研究考虑了气候变量,重点关注容器的结构特征、暴露和有机物。
elements_zh.main_results: 国内材料(41.9%)、盆(29.4%)和花盆(28.6%)的阳性率最高,而水壶和兽皮很少被定植。值得注意的是,虽然频率较低,但赤陶罐、桶、轮胎和杂项容器产生了 70% 以上的幼虫,将它们确定为主要生产地。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这证实了容器的结构特征,而不是其数量本身,决定了幼虫栖息地的适宜性。季节性也影响了幼虫的动态,在旱季,更多的容器呈阳性,但在雨季,平均密度高出三倍。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调了针对特定容器(特别是罐子、桶和轮胎)对 传播 风险最大的地区进行干预的重要性。将基于降雨的 监测 与社区主导的源头减少相结合可以加强控制工作。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于抽象证据,由于缺乏详细的统计分析以及未测量的混杂因素的潜在影响,研究结果的可信度较低。

papers.title: Integrating developmental traits, morphometrics and machine learning for sex classification of Aedes aegypti (Diptera: Culicidae).
papers.abstract: Abstract Aedes aegypti (Linnaeus, 1762), the primary vector for dengue, Zika, chikungunya and yellow fever, requires precise sex separation for the effective application of the sterile insect technique. This study integrates developmental biology, morphometric analysis and machine learning to differentiate sexes in Ae. aegypti pupae and adults. We evaluated developmental parameters across six generations of the Old Balara strain. Morphometric data from pupae and adults, including pupal cephalothorax dimensions, pupal length, pupal weight, adult wing length and adult thorax length, were collected to assess their correlations. Pupal morphometrics (cephalothorax dimensions and pupal length and weight) were used to train nine ML models for pupal sex classification. Males pupated significantly earlier (5.61 ± 0.10 days) than females (6.40 ± 0.16 days). In the absence of mating, females lived longer (22.63 ± 0.42 days) than males (20.13 ± 0.34 days). After mating, longevity declined, with females showing a 10.34% reduction (2.34 days) and males a 32.94% reduction (6.63 days). Across all morphometric parameters (cephalothorax length, width and perimeter in mm; cephalothorax area in mm 2 ; pupal length in mm; pupal weight in mg; adult wing length in mm; thorax length in mm), females were significantly larger than males. Pupal cephalothorax perimeter and area strongly correlated with adult thorax and wing lengths ( R 2 up to 0.88), indicating their predictive value for adult size. Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines and Naïve Bayes achieved 100% accuracy in pupal sex classification on the test set. Integrating morphometric analysis with machine learning significantly enhances sex sorting precision for the sterile insect technique, improving mosquito control efficiency by ensuring only males are released. Future research should explore incorporating image‐based data and advanced machine learning techniques to further refine these methods across diverse mosquito populations.

Males pupated significantly earlier (5.61 ± 0.10 days) than females (6.40 ± 0.16 days). In the absence of mating, females lived longer (22.63 ± 0.42 days) than males (20.13 ± 0.34 days). After mating, longevity declined, with females showing a 10.34% reduction (2.34 days) and males a 32.94% reduction (6.63 days). Across all morphometric parameters (cephalothorax length, width and perimeter in mm; cephalothorax area in mm 2 ; pupal length in mm; pupal weight in mg; adult wing length in mm; thorax length in mm), females were significantly larger than males. Pupal cephalothorax perimeter and area strongly correlated with adult thorax and wing lengths ( R 2 up to 0.88), indicating their predictive value for adult size. Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines and Naïve Bayes achieved 100% accuracy in pupal sex classification on the test set. Integrating morphometric analysis with machine learning significantly enhances sex sorting precision for the sterile insect technique, improving mosquito control efficiency by ensuring only males are released. Future research should explore incorporating image‐based data and advanced machine learning techniques to further refine these methods across diverse mosquito populations.

papers.title: Molecular Cloning and Reverse Genetics.
papers.abstract: This chapter describes a detailed molecular biology protocol for introducing specific point mutations into the chikungunya virus (CHIKV) genome using a reverse genetics strategy. The method utilizes an overlapping PCR-based approach to generate a mutated DNA fragment, which is then cloned into a pre-engineered CHIKV infectious clone plasmid. The protocol covers all major steps, from the initial PCRs to create the mutated insert to its digestion and ligation into the vector. It also includes procedures for bacterial transformation, colony screening via PCR and Sanger sequencing to confirm the mutation, and plasmid purification via miniprep. The document is structured with a clear introduction, a list of all required reagents and equipment, and a step-by-step methods section.

papers.title: Integrated multi-pathogen serosurveillance in children from East New Britain, Papua New Guinea using multiplex bead assays
papers.abstract: Children in Papua New Guinea experience a high burden of infectious diseases, including neglected tropical diseases, arboviral infections, enteric pathogens, and soil-transmitted helminths. Multi-pathogen serological surveillance provides a powerful approach for simultaneously characterising population-level exposure and susceptibility to multiple pathogens, complementing other forms of surveillance and to guide public health decision-making. We collected blood samples from 379 children aged 10 to 24 months (median 16 months) living in East New Britian Papua New Guinea, to assess antibodies to 11 priority pathogens. Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium (52.8%), followed by dengue (30.9%), chikungunya (25.3%), Giardia (13.5%) and malaria parasites (Plasmodium vivax 11.1%; Plasmodium falciparum 5.0%). Males were significantly more likely to be positive for trachoma (10.5% vs 2.2%, p = 0.001). Co-exposure to multiple pathogen groups was common, with approximately 45% of children seropositive for antibodies from two or more different pathogens. While prevalence varied markedly across pathogen groups, these results confirm substantial early-life exposure to multiple endemic pathogens in East New Britain, Papua New Guinea. Simultaneous assessment of multiple pathogens from a single sample demonstrates the value of multiplex serological surveillance and can inform targeted public health interventions.

By measuring pathogen-specific antibodies, serosurveys capture cumulative exposure 53 and immune responses that are often missed by conventional surveillance systems, particularly in low- 54 and middle-income settings. In Papua New Guinea (PNG), geographic, logistical, and health system 55 constraints limit the availability and representativeness of routine surveillance data, underscoring the 56 need for scalable approaches that can generate robust epidemiological evidence from existing studies 57 and specimens [2]. 58 Children in PNG experience a high burden of infectious diseases, including neglected tropical diseases, 59 arboviral infections, enteric pathogens, and soil-transmitted helminths, often with repeated or 60 3 concurrent exposures beginning early in life [3-6]. These infections are frequently asymptomatic or 61 underdiagnosed yet can have substantial cumulative impacts on child health. Chronic or recurrent 62 enteric infections and soil transmitted helminths have been associated with impaired linear growth, 63 undernutrition, anaemia, and altered immune function, while repeated arboviral and other endemic 64 infections may further contribute to inflammatory and immunological stress during critical periods of 65 development [7,8]. Understanding patterns of exposure to multiple pathogens in childhood is therefore 66 essential for informing integrated disease control strategies and broader child health interventions. 67 Multiplex bead assay (MBA) technologies enable the simultaneous measurement of antibodies to 68 antigens from multiple pathogens using a single, small-volume specimen. Integrating MBA-based 69 multi-pathogen serosurveillance into demographic health or disease-specific surveys allows efficient 70 assessment of exposure to vaccine preventable diseases, neglected tropical diseases, arboviruses, enteric 71 pathogens, and soil transmitted helminths within the same cohort [9]. This integrated approach supports 72 the identification of co-exposure patterns and overlapping disease burdens that would be difficult to 73 detect using pathogen-specific studies alone. As validated antigen targets continue to expand, MBA 74 platforms also facilitate cross-pathogen analytical approaches that can inform prioritisation of 75 interventions and contribute to efforts to reduce health inequities among children in PNG. 76 This study is a serological sub study nested within a larger study designed to assess population-level 77 immunity to vaccine-preventable diseases in young children in PNG. Leveraging stored samples from 78 the parent study provides a unique opportunity to extend the scientific value of existing data by 79 characterising exposure to a broader range of pathogens without additional sample collection or 80 participant burden [10]. Such an approach is particularly advantageous in paediatric populations, where 81 blood volumes are limited and repeated sampling is ethically and logistically challenging. 82 In this serological sub study, we investigated antibody seroprevalence to 20 antigens from 11 pathogens, 83 including neglected tropical diseases, soil transmitted helminths, malaria, arboviruses, and enteric 84 pathogens, among children aged 10 to 24 months residing in East New Britain Province (ENB), PNG. 85 Children were recruited from five priority local-level government (LLGs) areas encompassing urban, 86 rural, and remote island settings, selected to capture geographic and sociodemographic diversity across 87 4 ENB. This integrated, multi-pathogen approach provides a comprehensive assessment of early-life 88 exposure to endemic infections and generates evidence to inform coordinated child health and disease 89 control strategies in the province. 90 RESULTS 91 Demographic characteristics of the study participants is summarised in Table 1. A total of 379 children 92 aged 10-24 months, with a median age 16 months were enrolled between late March and mid-August 93 2023. Participant numbers were broadly comparable across the five targeted LLG areas, and just over 94 half of the cohort were male (53%). 95 Table 1: Demographic characteristics of participants 96 N (%) Gender Male 200 (53%) Female 179 (47%) Age (months) <12 70 (18%) 12 – <18 169 (45%) 18 – <24 136 (36%) Missing 4 (1%) Local-level government Bitapaka 78 (21%) Duke of York 77 (20%) Inland Baining 66 (17%) Kokopo Urban 81 (21%) Toma-Vunadidir 77 (20%) 97 98 99 100 5 Seroprevalence of pathogens in children 101 Among the 379 children, antibodies to multiple pathogens were detected, with substantial variation in 102 prevalence across the 11 pathogen groups included in the study (Supplementary Figure 1). 103 Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium (Cryptosporidium parvum) (52.8%), followed by 104 dengue virus (30.9%), chikungunya virus (25.3%), Giardia (Giardia lamblia) (13.5%), Plasmodium 105 vivax (11.1%), trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis) (6.6%), Plasmodium falciparum (5.0%), soil- 106 transmitted helminths (Strongyloides stercoralis or Taenia solium) (2.9%), lymphatic filariasis (1.9%), 107 Zika virus (1.6%) and yaws (Treponema pallidum) (0%). 108 No significant differences in seroprevalence were observed between males and females for most 109 pathogens. However, males were significantly more likely (10.5% vs 2.2%, p = 0.001) to have been 110 exposed to C. Trachomatis (Pgp3). Co-exposure to multiple pathogen groups was common. Of the 11 111 pathogens examined, approximately 25% (N = 93) of children were seropositive for antibodies from 112 two different pathogens, and an additional 20% (N = 77) were seropositive to three or more pathogens, 113 confirming significant exposure to malaria, arboviruses, and neglected tropical diseases in early 114 childhood. 115 116 Figure 1. Heatmap showing overall seroprevalence for the 11 pathogens examined in the study (N = 117 379). 118 6 Does exposure accumulate with age? 119 Serological responses demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in exposure across pathogens and age 120 groups. Antibody responses to Cryptosporidium were consistently high across all age strata, suggesting 121 that exposure occurs early in life. Similarly, seroreactivity to P. vivax was common across the study 122 population, indicating sustained transmission. 123 Clear age-related trends were observed for several pathogens. Seropositivity increased significantly 124 with age for yaws (p = 0.014), dengue virus (p < 0.001), and chikungunya virus (p < 0.001), indicative 125 of increased likelihood of environmental and vector exposure with age. (Figure 2). 126 For several infections, including trachoma (p = 0.035), P. falciparum, Giardia, and soil-transmitted 127 helminths, relatively high seroprevalence was observed among children younger than 12 months and 128 may reflect a combination of maternally derived antibodies and natural exposure. Consistent with this, 129 we observed a rise in seropositivity to P. falciparum, trachoma, Giardia in children aged >18 months, 130 but not 12-18 months, suggesting that antibody responses later in life reflect true exposure and infection 131 acquired during early childhood. 132 Pathogen-specific differences were also evident among the youngest infants. No serological evidence 133 of Zika virus exposure was detected in children younger than 12 months, while detectable antibodies 134 were observed in a small proportion of those children older than 12 months (1.6%). This finding 135 suggests either an absence of recent transmission or very limited exposure within the study population, 136 particularly among younger age groups. 137 138 139 7 140 141 Figure 2. Seroprevalence by age group (N = 379). 142 143 Where is transmission concentrated? 144 Seroprevalence varied across the five local-level government areas despite relatively similar numbers 145 of samples collected from each location, reflecting underlying geographic and sociodemographic 146 heterogeneity across the study sites, which included urban, rural, and remote island settings (Figure 3). 147 These spatial differences suggest heterogeneous patterns of pathogen exposure within the study 148 province. 149 Antibodies to P. vivax malaria were most prevalent in the Duke of York and Toma-Vunadidir LLGs, 150 indicating higher levels of exposure in these areas compared with the other study sites. In contrast, 151 serological evidence of trachoma (based on responses to C. trachomatis antigens) was markedly lower 152 in the Duke of York LLG. Arboviral exposure also showed geographic variation, with antibodies to 153 chikungunya most frequently detected among children living in the Bitapaka and Kokopo Urban LLGs. 154 8 Marked differences were also observed for several other pathogens. Notably, no serological evidence 155 of exposure to P. falciparum malaria or lymphatic filariasis was detected among children sampled from 156 the Inland Baining LLG. In contrast, almost half of children with antibodies to Giardia were from Toma- 157 Vunadidir, suggesting higher levels of transmission of this enteric pathogen in that area. Together, these 158 findings highlight substantial spatial heterogeneity in exposure to malaria, arboviruses, enteric 159 pathogens, and neglected tropical diseases within the study region. 160 161 162 163 164 165 166 167 168 169 170 171 172 173 174 175 176 177 178 179 180 181 9 182 Figure 3. Geographic variation in seroprevalence across five local-level governments (N = 379). 183 184 185 186 187 188 189 190 191 192 193 10 DISCUSSION 194 To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply integrated multi-pathogen serosurveillance in children 195 in PNG, demonstrating the feasibility and added value of this approach for characterising early life 196 exposure to multiple co-endemic pathogens in this setting. Overall, 45% of children had detectable 197 antibodies to multiple pathogens, although pathogen-specific seroprevalence varied by age and 198 geographic location. Seropositivity was highest for Cryptosporidium, followed by the arboviruses 199 dengue and chikungunya, then Giardia, trachoma, and malaria parasites P. vivax malaria and P. 200 falciparum malaria. Seroprevalence for dengue was similar to that of chikungunya, reflecting 201 comparable early-life exposure in this population. The high prevalence of antibodies to enteric 202 pathogens such as Cryptosporidium and Giardia suggests that exposure occurs very early in life, likely 203 reflecting ongoing transmission associated with limited access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene 204 conditions. While it is widely acknowledged that malaria, particularly Plasmodium vivax, is commonly 205 experienced by children in this age group in PNG [11,12], these findings provide serological evidence that 206 exposure to dengue and chikungunya is similarly prevalent. Data from Pacific Island serosurveys 207 support substantial dengue exposure occurring in early childhood, with seroprevalence among children 208 under five years already approaching 40–50% in some settings [13,14]. This is important for informing 209 both clinical management of febrile illness in young children and the design of targeted public health 210 interventions. 211 Overall, antibodies to enteric pathogens and malaria were most commonly detected, while neglected 212 tropical diseases such as soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma, yaws, and lymphatic filariasis were 213 generally less prevalent. Patterns of seropositivity varied across antigens, suggesting heterogeneous 214 transmission dynamics within the province and highlighting the value of multi-pathogen serological 215 surveillance in this young paediatric population. In 2022, East New Britain Province completed two 216 annual rounds of lymphatic filariasis mass drug administration with the triple drug regimen ivermectin, 217 diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole (IDA) [15]. The limited serological evidence of exposure observed 218 in this study of children surveyed in 2023 is consistent with reduced or interrupted transmission in two 219 LLGs [16]. The presence of detectable antibodies in a subset of children in 3 LLGs suggests that 220 11 transmission likely persists within some areas of ENB [16]. Seroprevalence was generally similar 221 between males and females, suggesting comparable exposure risks during early childhood. The 222 exception was the Pgp3 antigen of C. trachomatis, for which seropositivity was significantly higher in 223 males. This has not been previously observed in other studies of Pgp3 IgG seroprevalence to C. 224 trachomatis in children, which have identified age and community transmission intensity as they key 225 drivers of exposure [17]. Conversely, adult women have been reported to have substantially higher rates 226 of trachomatous scarring and trichiasis than men, widely attributed to gendered exposure over a lifetime 227 [18]. 228 Evidence of exposure to multiple pathogens was common. Approximately one-quarter of children were 229 seropositive for antibodies to two pathogens, and a further one-fifth showed evidence of exposure to 230 three or more pathogens. This pattern highlights the considerable infectious disease burden faced by 231 young children in this setting, where malaria parasites, arboviruses, enteric pathogens, and neglected 232 tropical diseases circulate concurrently. The age-stratified analyses further support this interpretation. 233 Seropositivity increased with age for several pathogens, including dengue, chikungunya, lymphatic 234 filariasis, and yaws, consistent with increasing interaction with people, vectors or environment as 235 children get older. In contrast, seroreactivity to Cryptosporidium remained high across age groups, 236 suggesting that exposure occurs very early in life. papers.title: Bionomics aspects of major arbovirus vectors, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus in different ecoclimatic environments of Cameroon
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Aedes mosquitoes transmit dengue, Zika and chikungunya viruses, which remain major public health concerns globally and in Africa. Effective prevention and control rely on a sound understanding of vector bio-ecology. In Cameroon, little is known about the bio-ecology and behaviour of Aedes vectors. This study aimed to update the geographical distribution, resting behaviour, host-seeking behaviour and natural infections by arboviruses in Aedes spp. vectors in Cameroon. Methods Sampling was carried out in eight locations across the country. Immature stages of Aedes were collected in seven localities, transported to the insectary, reared to adult, identified, counted, and grouped by species to determine their distribution. Resting behaviour was assessed through inside houses and outdoor aspirations using Prokopack and CDC backpack aspirators. Host-seeking activity was evaluated with BG-Sentinel traps. Natural infections with dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses were determined by real-time quantitative Multiplex PCR and RT-PCR. Chi-squared test was used to compare abundances Results 17,040 adults identified from the immature stages of Aedes spp. albopictus , 48.93% Ae. aegypti , and 0.02% Ae. We noted the first identification of Aedes albopictus in Meiganga since its introduction in Cameroon. Aedes aegypti was present in all the localities surveyed, while Ae. albopictus had a distribution limited to the southern part of the country below latitude 6.4°N. Resting and biting behaviours have shown that both species are essentially exophilic and exophagous. Aedes aegypti preferred to rest in used tyres, while Ae. albopictus had a wide range of preferred resting sites (natural vegetation, used tyres, banana plants, mixed resting places). Both species of mosquito bite throughout the day between 6 a.m. to 7 p.m., with essentially unimodal host-seeking activity, with a major peak of activity in the afternoon between 1 p.m. Natural infections by dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses showed one positive pool of Ae. aegypti for serotype 3 of dengue virus (DENV-3). Conclusion These results provide an important knowledge base on the bionomics of Aedes mosquitoes in different localities in Cameroon and also establish evidence base essential for designing and implementing targeted arboviral diseases surveillance and vector control strategies.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在更新伊蚊属虫媒病毒的地理分布、静息行为、宿主 寻找行为和自然感染。在喀麦隆,解决该国对这些 媒介 缺乏了解的问题。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及在喀麦隆全国八个地点对伊蚊属的未成熟阶段进行采样。收集并饲养成虫以进行识别和分布分析。使用各种方法评估休息和寻找 宿主 的行为,并确定登革热、基孔肯雅热和寨卡病毒的自然感染。
elements_zh.methods: 在七个地点收集了未成熟阶段的昆虫,运输到昆虫饲养场,饲养成成虫并进行鉴定。使用 Prokopack 和 CDC 背包吸气器通过室内和室外呼吸来评估休息行为。使用 BG-Sentinel 陷阱评估 宿主 寻找活动。通过实时定量多重 PCR 和 RT-PCR 确定虫媒病毒的自然感染。
elements_zh.main_results: 鉴定出未成熟期伊蚊成虫17,040只,其中伊蚊占48.93%。埃及伊蚊和 0.02% Ae。所有调查地点均存在埃及伊蚊,而伊蚊则存在于所有调查地点。白纹伊蚊在该国南部地区发现。两个物种均表现出嗜外食性和外食性行为,其中 Ae.埃及伊蚊更喜欢二手轮胎和埃及伊蚊。白纹伊蚊有广泛的首选栖息地。单个 Ae 阳性池。已鉴定出携带 DENV-3 的埃及伊蚊。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究提供了有关喀麦隆不同地区伊蚊生物学特性的重要知识,为设计和实施有针对性的虫媒病毒性疾病 监测 和 媒介 控制策略奠定了证据基础。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可为喀麦隆虫媒病毒疾病 监测、诊断 和 媒介 控制策略提供信息,通过增强对 媒介 生物生态学的了解,为公共卫生做出贡献。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因使用非随机抽样方法且缺乏详细的统计分析而受到限制。由于该研究的观察性质,证据强度中等。

Both species of mosquito bite throughout the day between 6 a.m. to 7 p.m., with essentially unimodal host-seeking activity, with a major peak of activity in the afternoon between 1 p.m. Natural infections by dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses showed one positive pool of Ae. aegypti for serotype 3 of dengue virus (DENV-3). papers.title: Emerging or Newly Detected? Rethinking Infectious Disease Outbreaks in North Africa
papers.abstract: North Africa sits where climate change, armed conflict and cross-border mobility meet, and each of these moves pathogens. Yet outbreaks in the region are often recognized late, through travel surveillance abroad, single-hospital studies or reference laboratories rather than routine national reporting. This editorial, which opens the special issue on emerging and re-emerging infectious disease outbreaks in North Africa, reviews three microbial fronts: arboviruses such as West Nile, dengue and chikungunya viruses; antimicrobial resistance and conflict-driven cholera; and fungal pathogens, including Candida auris. It summarizes eleven outbreaks reported in the region since 2012 and how each came to light. The gap between reported and actual burden can be large: in eastern Sudan in 2018, surveillance counted 13,978 chikungunya cases, whereas the epidemic was later estimated to have affected about 487,600 people. The editorial argues that many infections called emerging in North Africa are newly detected rather than new, and that the main gap lies in laboratory and surveillance capacity. It calls for integrated One Health surveillance and wider access to molecular and fungal diagnostics.

papers.abstract_zh: 北非位于气候变化、武装冲突和跨境流动交汇的地方,每一种因素都会传播病原体。然而,该地区的 暴发 通常通过出国旅行、单家医院研究或参考实验室而不是常规的国家报告而较晚得到认可。这篇社论开启了关于北非新出现和重新出现的传染病 暴发 的特刊,回顾了三个微生物前沿:西尼罗河、登革热和 基孔肯雅病毒 等虫媒病毒;抗菌素耐药性和冲突引发的霍乱;和真菌病原体,包括耳念珠菌。它总结了自 2012 年以来该地区报告的 11 起 暴发 事件以及每起事件的曝光过程。报告的负担与实际负担之间的差距可能很大:2018 年,监测 统计在苏丹东部有 13,978 例基孔肯雅热病例,而后来估计该流行病影响了约 487,600 人。社论认为,许多被称为北非新出现的感染是新发现的而不是新的,主要差距在于实验室和 监测 的能力。它呼吁整合 One Health 监测 以及更广泛地获得分子和真菌诊断。

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 这篇社论探讨了北非传染病的出现和重新出现,重点关注 基孔肯雅病毒 及其相关谱系。它探讨了如何识别 暴发 以及准确评估其真实负担的挑战。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该审查基于自 2012 年以来该地区报告的 11 个 暴发 中的 暴发。这些 暴发 根据检测方式进行了总结,强调了对旅行 监测、单家医院研究和参考实验室而不是常规国家报告的依赖。

papers.title: Screening of Antiviral Agents Against CHIKV Using Reporter Virus.
papers.abstract: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) causes a disease characterized by chronic musculoskeletal inflammation for which specific antivirals are not yet available. Currently, a supportive therapy to alleviate fever and pain is used, but it does not limit viral replication or the persistence of chronic arthritis symptoms. Thus, the identification and development of new active molecules against CHIKV is urgently needed. Here, we present a cell-based methodology that enables the implementation of a rapid and cost-effective strategy for high- and medium-throughput screening (HTS) of compounds, including repurposed drugs or novel molecules. This methodology allows for the identification of novel antiviral hits with a good activity and selectivity profile against CHIKV.

papers.title: Epitope Tagging and Coimmunoprecipitation to Identify Viral Protein Interactors.
papers.abstract: Affinity purification-mass spectrometry (AP-MS) is a powerful proteomic approach for dissecting the interaction network between virus and host. Traditional AP-MS employs overexpression of viral proteins as baits to enrich host interactors. However, overexpressed viral proteins may mislocalize to inappropriate cellular compartments and trigger endoplasmic reticulum stress by overwhelming the protein-folding machinery, which leads to false identification of host factors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an AP-MS strategy based on direct infection with an epitope-tagged chikungunya virus (CHIKV/myc-E2), which we used to successfully uncover two new antiviral factors in CHIKV cellular reservoirs-macrophages. In this protocol, we will describe this technique step by step: (1) design and construction of myc-tagged virus by advanced multi-fragment assembly, (2) in vitro transcription and preparation of infectious myc-tagged virus stocks, and (3) immunoprecipitation of myc-tagged viral protein and its interactome for mass spectrometry analysis. This strategy enables accurate identification of viral interactors in a physiologically relevant context, providing a framework for future proteomic studies using tagged viruses.

However, overexpressed viral proteins may mislocalize to inappropriate cellular compartments and trigger endoplasmic reticulum stress by overwhelming the protein-folding machinery, which leads to false identification of host factors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an AP-MS strategy based on direct infection with an epitope-tagged chikungunya virus (CHIKV/myc-E2), which we used to successfully uncover two new antiviral factors in CHIKV cellular reservoirs-macrophages. In this protocol, we will describe this technique step by step: (1) design and construction of myc-tagged virus by advanced multi-fragment assembly, (2) in vitro transcription and preparation of infectious myc-tagged virus stocks, and (3) immunoprecipitation of myc-tagged viral protein and its interactome for mass spectrometry analysis. This strategy enables accurate identification of viral interactors in a physiologically relevant context, providing a framework for future proteomic studies using tagged viruses.

papers.title: A Restriction-Free Cloning Approach for Molecular Engineering of Plasmids.
papers.abstract: Molecular cloning by PCR amplification using a highly processive, high-fidelity DNA polymerase represents a robust and versatile technique for the precise manipulation of nucleic acid sequences. This approach enables the insertion, replacement, or modification of specific DNA fragments within a cloning vector, thereby generating an accurate copy of a gene or viral segment for downstream applications, such as protein expression, site-directed mutagenesis, and structural or functional analyses. The use of processive, high-fidelity polymerases significantly reduces the occurrence of base substitution errors, ensuring sequence integrity throughout the amplification process. Traditionally, restriction enzymes have been employed to facilitate directional cloning; however, alternative methods allow for mutagenesis without the need for unique and specific restriction sites and can be applied to virtually any cloning or seamless DNA assembly strategy. In this chapter, we describe a restriction enzyme-free and ligation-free PCR-based protocol widely applicable to any circular vector. This method enables targeted mutagenesis of the chikungunya virus (CHIKV) genome, offering a fast, efficient, and reliable strategy for generating mutant constructs suitable for virological and molecular studies.

papers.title_zh: 质粒分子工程的无限制克隆方法。
papers.source_body_en: Molecular cloning by PCR amplification using a highly processive, high-fidelity DNA polymerase represents a robust and versatile technique for the precise manipulation of nucleic acid sequences. This approach enables the insertion, replacement, or modification of specific DNA fragments within a cloning vector, thereby generating an accurate copy of a gene or viral segment for downstream applications, such as protein expression, site-directed mutagenesis, and structural or functional analyses. The use of processive, high-fidelity polymerases significantly reduces the occurrence of base substitution errors, ensuring sequence integrity throughout the amplification process. Traditionally, restriction enzymes have been employed to facilitate directional cloning; however, alternative methods allow for mutagenesis without the need for unique and specific restriction sites and can be applied to virtually any cloning or seamless DNA assembly strategy. In this chapter, we describe a restriction enzyme-free and ligation-free PCR-based protocol widely applicable to any circular vector. This method enables targeted mutagenesis of the chikungunya virus (CHIKV) genome, offering a fast, efficient, and reliable strategy for generating mutant constructs suitable for virological and molecular studies.

papers.title: Analysis of Cell Populations from Arbovirus-Infected Tissues by Flow Cytometry.
papers.abstract: Arboviruses still represent a major challenge to public health in many parts of the world. Despite shared epidemiological characteristics, each arboviral disorder displays distinct cellular tropism and activation patterns, progressing to immunopathological outcomes that remain not fully elucidated. A deeper understanding of these processes requires methodologies capable of characterizing the often-complex cellular responses. In this context, flow cytometry emerges as a valuable tool, enabling the characterization of heterogeneous cell populations, the assessment of activation and proliferation markers, the quantification of inflammatory mediators, and the detection of cell death pathways. By integrating these parameters, flow cytometry can enhance our understanding of arbovirus pathogenesis, clarify their cellular tropism, and understand immune responses to infection. This methodological article outlines the main steps for applying the technique to different target tissues infected by chikungunya, dengue, yellow fever, and Zika viruses, emphasizing the most effective strategies.

papers.title: Beyond long COVID: post-acute infection syndromes across Africa, a systematic review
papers.abstract: Post-acute infection syndromes (PAIS) have gained global attention through Long COVID, yet many pathogens most closely linked to PAIS are endemic to Africa, where evidence remains scarce; a gap with implications for health equity and global health security. We aimed to systematically review the prevalence, clinical presentation, and associated factors of PAIS following non-COVID infections in Africa, and to identify priorities for future research. We conducted a systematic review, searching Medline, Embase, and grey literature until 7 November 2025 for studies in Africa reporting symptoms four or more weeks after acute infection. Case reports, case series, conference abstracts, secondary research, comments, and correspondence were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data on study characteristics, symptom prevalence, clinical presentation, and associated factors. As substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies, results were summarised descriptively. The study was registered on the Open Science Framework. Of 1,368 records, 65 studies were included, 42 on Ebola virus disease and 19 on chikungunya, with moderate to low risk of bias. Prevalence of PAIS ranged from 17.5% to 98.6% after Ebola and 12.1% to 78.6% after chikungunya. Musculoskeletal pain, ocular complications, headache, and fatigue predominated after Ebola; arthralgia was the hallmark of post-chikungunya disease. Substantial symptom burden persisted years after acute infection. Female sex, older age, and greater acute disease severity were the factors most frequently reported to be associated with persistent sequelae. An exploratory, non-systematic supplementary search additionally identified sex-specific consequences among female survivors including menstrual irregularities and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Despite scarce, heterogeneous, and geographically concentrated evidence, the reported prevalence of persistent symptoms among survivors is high, although the absence of comparison groups in most studies complicates attribution to the infection itself. Health systems in Africa must adapt to provide long-term survivor care, embedding follow-up into existing chronic care platforms. As pathogens endemic to Africa carry pandemic potential and expand geographically, understanding their chronic consequences is both a matter of health equity and an urgent global health security priority.

papers.title: Development of a One-Step RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b Assay for Rapid On-Site Detection of Dabie Bandavirus
papers.abstract: Abstract Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by Dabie bandavirus (DBV), has rapidly spread to multiple countries worldwide since its discovery in 2009, posing a serious threat to global public health security. SFTS is a tick-borne disease, and people living in mountainous and hilly areas are at increased risk of infection, which highlights the urgent need for rapid, accurate, and field-applicable diagnostic strategies for DBV. In this study, LAMP primers and CRISPR sgRNA were designed based on the conserved region of the DBV L segment. A one-pot, one-step molecular assay integrating reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP) with CRISPR/Cas12b technology was established after systematic optimization of key parameters. The assay operates under isothermal conditions at 60 °C, delivering results within 40 min. Analytical evaluation demonstrated a limit of detection of 25.6 RNA copies per reaction. No cross-reactivity was observed with Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Chikungunya virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, Dengue virus, and Zika virus. Clinical validation using 42 specimens showed complete concordance with gold-standard qRT-PCR, achieving 100% sensitivity (30/30) and 100% specificity (12/12). For point-of-care application, fluorescence visualization was incorporated into the CRISPR/Cas-based detection workflow, enabling straightforward result interpretation. This integrated RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b platform provides rapid and specific detection of DBV through a simplified workflow that does not require complex instrumentation, supporting its potential application in resource-limited environments.

For point-of-care application, fluorescence visualization was incorporated into the CRISPR/Cas-based detection workflow, enabling straightforward result interpretation. This integrated RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b platform provides rapid and specific detection of DBV through a simplified workflow that does not require complex instrumentation, supporting its potential application in resource-limited environments.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 由大别班达病毒(DBV)引起的发热伴血小板减少综合征(SFTS)自2009年发现以来已迅速蔓延至全球多个国家,对全球公共卫生安全构成严重威胁。SFTS 是一种蜱传疾病,生活在山区和丘陵地区的人们感染的风险增加,这凸显了对 DBV 快速、准确和现场适用的诊断策略的迫切需要。本研究根据DBV L片段的保守区域设计了LAMP引物和CRISPR sgRNA。经过系统优化关键参数后,建立了一种将逆转录环介导等温扩增(RT-LAMP)与CRISPR/Cas12b技术相结合的一锅一步式分子检测方法。该测定在 60 °C 等温条件下进行,可在 40 分钟内得出结果。分析评估表明每个反应的检测限为 25.6 个 RNA 拷贝。未观察到与汉滩病毒、首尔病毒、基孔肯雅病毒、日本脑炎病毒、登革热病毒和寨卡病毒的交叉反应。使用 42 个样本进行的临床验证显示与金标准 qRT-PCR 完全一致,实现了 100% 的敏感性 (30/30) 和 100% 的特异性 (12/12)。对于现场护理应用,荧光可视化被纳入基于 CRISPR/Cas 的检测工作流程,从而实现简单的结果解释。这种集成的 RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b 平台通过简化的工作流程提供 DBV 的快速、特异性检测,不需要复杂的仪器,支持其在资源有限的环境中的潜在应用。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在针对大别班达病毒(DBV)开发一种快速、准确且适用于现场的诊断策略,该病毒会导致严重发热伴血小板减少综合征(SFTS),对全球公共卫生安全构成严重威胁。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究设计并优化了一种用于 DBV 检测的一步式 RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b 检测方法,重点关注 DBV L 片段的保守区域,并使用 42 个临床标本对其进行了验证。
analysis_zh.methods: LAMP引物和CRISPR sgRNA是根据DBV L片段的保守区域设计的。该测定经过优化,可在 60 °C 等温条件下运行,40 分钟内即可得出结果。临床验证显示 100% 的敏感性和特异性。
analysis_zh.main_results: 该检测显示每次反应的检测限为 25.6 个 RNA 拷贝,并且未显示与其他病毒的交叉反应。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 集成的 RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b 平台通过简化的工作流程提供 DBV 的快速、特异性检测,支持其在资源有限环境中的潜在应用。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该检测可以改善 SFTS 的 诊断,这对于及时 诊断 和控制疾病至关重要,特别是在人们风险较高的山区和丘陵地区。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究没有报告任何设计限制或偏见,证据强度很高。

papers.full_text: Abstract Background Aedes aegypti is a primary vector of Dengue, Chikungunya, and Zika viruses, and its control relies heavily on pyrethroid insecticides. However, the development of resistance in mosquito populations poses a major challenge to effective vector control. This study aimed to investigate the presence of the V1016G knockdown resistance (kdr) mutation in Aedes aegypti collected from Nagapattinam district, Tamil Nadu, India. Methods Aedes immatures were collected from selected field sites and subjected to insecticide susceptibility testing using World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines. Genomic DNA was extracted, and allele-specific PCR was performed to detect the V1016G mutation in the voltage-gated sodium channel gene (vgsc). Results The analysis revealed the presence of the V1016G mutation in heterozygous form (VG) among the tested samples. No homozygous mutants (GG) were detected. The presence of heterozygous individuals indicates an early stage of resistance development, likely due to ongoing insecticide selection pressure. Bioassay results showed reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids in these populations, supporting the molecular findings. Conclusion This study provides baseline data on the genetic mechanism of pyrethroid resistance in Aedes aegypti from Nagapattinam district. Regular monitoring of kdr mutations is essential to detect resistance early and guide insecticide use policies. Integrating molecular surveillance with conventional control measures will help delay the spread of resistance and improve the long-term success of vector management programs. The findings highlight the need for alternative control strategies and responsible insecticide use to maintain the effectiveness of current interventions. Methods included genomic DNA extraction and allele-specific PCR to detect the mutation, alongside insecticide susceptibility testing using WHO guidelines. Results showed the V1016G mutation in heterozygous form but no homozygous mutants, with bioassays confirming reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids. The study provides baseline data for molecular surveillance of resistance in Aedes aegypti, highlighting the need for integrated control strategies. However, the study's limitations include a lack of generalisability and detailed statistical analysis, resulting in moderate confidence in the evidence.

papers.full_text: BACKGROUND Aedes vittatus, an emerging invasive species and arboviral vector with high ecological plasticity and dispersal capacity, is expanding in the Caribbean, being detected in the Dominican Republic, Cuba, and Jamaica and recently in Yucatán, Mexico.OBJECTIVESThis study aimed to provide evidence of the establishment of Ae. vittatus in Haiti.METHODSLarval surveys were conducted in 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti. Specimens were identified morphologically and confirmed by COI-based DNA barcoding.FINDINGSWe report, for the first time, the detection of the invasive vector Ae. (Fredwardsius) vittatus in Haiti, confirmed morphologically and molecularly, with the species detected in half of the municipalities sampled. Phylogenetic analyses placed Haitian specimens within a Caribbean/American group, closely related to sequences from Mexico. Additional mosquito species were identified, including first records of Culex garciai and Culex interrogator in Haiti.MAIN CONCLUSIONSGiven its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas are needed. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study area - The survey was conducted in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti, restricted to the extensive, low-elevation coastal zones of both regions. Mosquito larvae were collected from peridomestic and public spaces. For each sample site, some collected larvae were mounted on slides, while others were reared to the adult stage, and both types of specimens were deposited in the ARIM-IRD collection.( 7 ) Geographical coordinates and data were uploaded to the GBIF platform.Fig. 1:location of the sampling sites. (A) Situation map of Haiti within Caribbean countries with presence (green area) and location of capture points (red dots) of Aedes vittatus in neighbouring countries; (B) Delimitation of study area in Haiti (blue rectangle) and location capture (red dots) of Ae. vittatus in Haiti and the Dominican Republic; (C) Location of the breeding site of Ae. vittatus in the study area (red dots) and other collection sites negative to Ae. vittatus (grey dots) (Table). Morphological and molecular identification - The invasive species Ae. vittatus was identified using European,( 8 ) African( 9 ) and Sahelian( 10 ) taxonomic keys, and confirmed with the species redescription of Huang.( 11 ) Five samples from the localities Quartier Morin (two adults: QUA003-Haiti06 and 07) and Lory, Milot (two adults: MIL001-Haiti08 and 09 and one larvae: MIL004LAV-10) were used for molecular identification. diagnostic characters for the principal life stages for Ae. vittatus are summarised as follows (Fig. 2).Fig. 2: Aedes vittatus: morphological characteristics of the larval stage. (A) Detail of abdominal segments VIII-X (the long anal papillae are missing); (B) head showing single setae 5-C and 6-C (arrows); (C) mentum; (D) comb VIII with eight spines; (E) detail of the pecten teeth with two or three denticles; (F) atypical pecten with the rare presence of two teeth (instead of one, arrows) inserted distal to the 1-S setae. Female - Head with a dark proboscis with a median scattering of pale yellowish scales. Thorax: scutum with acrostichal setae; three pairs of distinct, small, white spots of narrow scales on the anterior two-thirds of the scutum; scutellum with broad white scales on all three lobes; lower mesepimeral setae present. Legs: tibia with a median white ring, tarsomeres III-1-4 with large basal white bands, tarsomere III-5 entirely white. Abdomen: tergite I with a large median white spot. Male genitalia - Gonocoxite elongated, without basal and apical lobes. The gonostyle has a very characteristic shape, strongly enlarged and globose at its tip, with a long, strongly curved apical spine located at the base of the globose part. The claspette is large, with a narrow base, and distinctly swollen from its middle. Larva (Fig. 2) - Head: setae 5-C single or sometimes double, 6-C single. Abdomen: setae 6-I-IV usually with two long branches; pecten with 19-25 very closely spaced spines, with 3-4 basal denticles; only the most distal spine (rarely two) more widely spaced and implanted beyond seta 1-S; comb of eight (6-10) scales in a single irregular row; saddle incomplete without marginal spicules; 1-X single, 2-X with 5 branches; four precratal setae; anal papillae long, about four times as long as saddle, slender and tapered. The Ae. vittatus specimens (Haiti_06, Haiti_07, Haiti_08, Haiti_09) clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico).( 3 , 5 (24-27) In the haplotype network, they share closely related haplotypes separated by only a small number of mutations, suggesting a high level of genetic similarity within this group, particularly with Mexican populations( 5 ) (Fig. 3). This Caribbean/American cluster appeared distinct from African haplotypes and from most Asian haplotypes, which form separate groups within the network. The observed pattern is consistent with the Caribbean/American lineage being genetically distinct from African and most Asian haplotypes, although the limited number of specimens and the use of a single mitochondrial marker preclude firm conclusions about the geographic origin or pathways of introduction. The COI-based DNA barcoding confirmed the identification of Ps. pygmaea, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus and Cx. interrogator, with the latter showing high similarity to GenBank reference sequences (99.67% identity; MT999299.1). Sequences of Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, Cx. garciai, Cx. interrogator, Cx. quinquefasciatus and Ps. pygmaea have been deposited under accession numbers PZ878903, PZ878904, PZ878905, PZ878906, PZ878907, PZ878908, PZ878909, PZ878910, PZ878911.Fig. 3:haplotype network and phylogenetic tree resulting from the analysis of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I barcoding region (COI) dataset. The haplotype network reconstruction considers missing data and gap. Values between parentheses on nodes indicate the inferred number of mutation steps between haplotypes or ancestral haplotypes (symbolised by a black node). The phylogenetic tree corresponds to the results of a Bayesian inference analysis (see text for details). DISCUSSIONSpecies identification was confirmed morphologically and by COI-based DNA barcoding. Haitian Ae. vittatus specimens clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, Dominican Republic, and Mexico) and were clearly distinct from African and most Asian lineages (Fig. 3). This pattern is consistent with a shared regional genetic background within the Caribbean/American group, although more molecular markers, more populations and specimens are needed to confirm this hypothesis. Detection of Ae. vittatus in one-third of the sampled habitats and half of the surveyed communes, despite limited sampling, indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti. However, given the limited sampling effort, further surveys are needed to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.Its absence from earlier surveys in 2013,( 6 ) combined with its detection in the Dominican Republic in 2019,( 3 ) is consistent with a relatively recent arrival on Hispaniola. However, the available data do not allow us to determine the timing or pathway of introduction. Passive transport via water holding containers and other goods may have contributed to its spread, but the relative importance of each introduction pathway remains unknown. Passive transport via water-holding goods is a well-documented pathway for mosquito invasions, and the species’ desiccation-resistant eggs further enhance its dispersal potential. Genetic similarity with recently detected Mexican populations( 5 ) suggests strong regional connectivity, although the direction of spread remains unclear. Additional sampling across Haiti and the use of nuclear and/or genomic markers will be necessary to clarify the distribution, population structure and introduction pathways of the species.Current socio-environmental conditions in Haiti, including population displacement, informal settlements, inadequate water infrastructure, and unmanaged waste, favour the proliferation of container-breeding mosquitoes and may provide favourable conditions for the establishment of Ae. vittatus. full_text_sections.abstract: BACKGROUND Aedes vittatus, an emerging invasive species and arboviral vector with high ecological plasticity and dispersal capacity, is expanding in the Caribbean, being detected in the Dominican Republic, Cuba, and Jamaica and recently in Yucatán, Mexico.OBJECTIVESThis study aimed to provide evidence of the establishment of Ae. vittatus in Haiti.METHODSLarval surveys were conducted in 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti. Specimens were identified morphologically and confirmed by COI-based DNA barcoding.FINDINGSWe report, for the first time, the detection of the invasive vector Ae. (Fredwardsius) vittatus in Haiti, confirmed morphologically and molecularly, with the species detected in half of the municipalities sampled. Phylogenetic analyses placed Haitian specimens within a Caribbean/American group, closely related to sequences from Mexico. Additional mosquito species were identified, including first records of Culex garciai and Culex interrogator in Haiti.MAIN CONCLUSIONSGiven its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas are needed.
