The Ae. vittatus specimens (Haiti_06, Haiti_07, Haiti_08, Haiti_09) clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico).( 3 , 5 (24-27) In the haplotype network, they share closely related haplotypes separated by only a small number of mutations, suggesting a high level of genetic similarity within this group, particularly with Mexican populations( 5 ) (Fig. 3). This Caribbean/American cluster appeared distinct from African haplotypes and from most Asian haplotypes, which form separate groups within the network. The observed pattern is consistent with the Caribbean/American lineage being genetically distinct from African and most Asian haplotypes, although the limited number of specimens and the use of a single mitochondrial marker preclude firm conclusions about the geographic origin or pathways of introduction. The COI-based DNA barcoding confirmed the identification of Ps. pygmaea, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus and Cx. interrogator, with the latter showing high similarity to GenBank reference sequences (99.67% identity; MT999299.1). For Cx. garciai, no reference sequences are currently available in GenBank; therefore, we generated the first COI sequences for this species in this study. Sequences of Ae. vittatus were submitted to GenBank under accession numbers PZ344144, PZ344145, PZ344146 and PZ344147. Sequences of Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, Cx. garciai, Cx. interrogator, Cx. quinquefasciatus and Ps. pygmaea have been deposited under accession numbers PZ878903, PZ878904, PZ878905, PZ878906, PZ878907, PZ878908, PZ878909, PZ878910, PZ878911.Fig. 3:haplotype network and phylogenetic tree resulting from the analysis of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I barcoding region (COI) dataset. The haplotype network reconstruction considers missing data and gap. Values between parentheses on nodes indicate the inferred number of mutation steps between haplotypes or ancestral haplotypes (symbolised by a black node). The phylogenetic tree corresponds to the results of a Bayesian inference analysis (see text for details).
full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONSpecies identification was confirmed morphologically and by COI-based DNA barcoding. Haitian Ae. vittatus specimens clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, Dominican Republic, and Mexico) and were clearly distinct from African and most Asian lineages (Fig. 3). This pattern is consistent with a shared regional genetic background within the Caribbean/American group, although more molecular markers, more populations and specimens are needed to confirm this hypothesis. Detection of Ae. vittatus in one-third of the sampled habitats and half of the surveyed communes, despite limited sampling, indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti. However, given the limited sampling effort, further surveys are needed to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.Its absence from earlier surveys in 2013,( 6 ) combined with its detection in the Dominican Republic in 2019,( 3 ) is consistent with a relatively recent arrival on Hispaniola. However, the available data do not allow us to determine the timing or pathway of introduction. Passive transport via water holding containers and other goods may have contributed to its spread, but the relative importance of each introduction pathway remains unknown. Passive transport via water-holding goods is a well-documented pathway for mosquito invasions, and the species’ desiccation-resistant eggs further enhance its dispersal potential. Genetic similarity with recently detected Mexican populations( 5 ) suggests strong regional connectivity, although the direction of spread remains unclear. Additional sampling across Haiti and the use of nuclear and/or genomic markers will be necessary to clarify the distribution, population structure and introduction pathways of the species.Current socio-environmental conditions in Haiti, including population displacement, informal settlements, inadequate water infrastructure, and unmanaged waste, favour the proliferation of container-breeding mosquitoes and may provide favourable conditions for the establishment of Ae. vittatus. The species exhibits high ecological plasticity, colonising a wide range of artificial and natural habitats. Its tolerance to desiccation, salinity, and high temperatures further enhances its invasion potential.( 28 ) Co-occurrence with Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus raises questions about interspecific interactions and future ecological dynamics in urban environments. Notably, we also reported Cx. garciai and Cx. interrogator from Haiti for the first time. Morphological identification of Cx. interrogator was supported by molecular results, showing high sequence identity but lower query coverage, likely reflecting partial sequences or trimming.From a public health perspective, Ae. vittatus is competent for multiple arboviruses, including dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever.( 29 , 30 ) Its establishment adds complexity to Haiti’s epidemiologic context, which already includes endemic dengue, recurrent chikungunya outbreaks, and ongoing malaria and filariasis transmission. Notably, ecological niche models suggest that Ae. vittatus could find year-round suitable conditions across coastal regions of the Gulf of Mexico and extend into the southern Atlantic states of the United States, as well as large areas of Mexico and Central America.( 31 ) This potential geographic suitability highlights the possibility of further spread into North America, Central and South America and underscores the need for strengthened surveillance and preparedness beyond the Caribbean.Our findings provide the first confirmed record of Ae. vittatus in Haiti and demonstrate its presence in multiple locations. Further surveillance is needed to determine its distribution, extent of establishment, ecological interactions, and potential contribution to arbovirus transmission in the region and beyond.
full_text_sections.other: REVIEWER #1The abstract adequately summarizes the study and highlights the first detection of Aedes vittatus in Haiti. This finding fills an important geographical gap and has clear relevance for mosquito surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas. The manuscript should avoid strong conclusions, as these interpretations are based on limited sampling and a single mitochondrial marker. Inconsistencies in dates and sites / localities should also be corrected. References are generally relevant and updated, but their formatting should be standardized. AUTHORS’ RESPONSE TO THE REVIEWERSDear Prof. Ricardo Lourenço-de-Oliveira and Maria Clara Carvalho:We are pleased to submit the letter of response to the referees for the manuscript entitled “Aedes vittatus in Haiti: continued expansion across the Caribbean and implications for the Americas” for consideration in Memórias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz, on behalf of my co-authors. Here are our point-by-point responses. The comments are in bold and our responses are in regular text in blue. We have added the modifications to a track changes version of the manuscript in red.Reviewer comments:The abstract adequately summarizes the study and highlights the first detection of Aedes vittatus in Haiti. This finding fills an important geographical gap and has clear relevance for mosquito surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas.We sincerely thank you for your positive and constructive and positive comments. We are pleased that you find the study relevant and that the detection of Aedes vittatus in Haiti fills an important geographical gap for mosquito surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas.The manuscript should avoid strong conclusions, as these interpretations are based on limited sampling and a single mitochondrial marker.We agree and we have moderated the strength of our conclusions throughout the manuscript, particularly in the Abstract and Discussion, to better reflect the limitations of our study, including the relatively limited sampling effort and the use of a single mitochondrial marker (COI). We now explicitly acknowledge these limitations and clarify that our interpretations regarding establishment, regional expansion and spread should be considered with caution.In the abstract, we changed for: “We report, for the first time, the detection of the invasive vector Aedes (Fredwardsius) vittatus in Haiti, confirmed morphologically and molecularly, with the species detected in half of the municipalities sampled. Phylogenetic analyses placed Haitian specimens within a Caribbean/American group, closely related to sequences from Mexico.” (lines 31-34). Also in the main conclusion of the abstract: “Given its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas are needed.” (lines 35-36).In the results, we substitute the sentence: “The results support a common Asian-rather than African or European origin with regional spread in the Caribbean.”, with “The observed pattern is consistent with the Caribbean/American lineage being genetically distinct from African and most Asian haplotypes, although the limited number of specimens and the use of a single mitochondrial marker preclude firm conclusions about the geographic origin or pathways of introduction.” (lines 172-176).In the conclusion, we substitute: “This pattern supports a shared regional origin and spread within the Caribbean rather than multiple independent introductions from the Old World.”, for “This pattern is consistent with a shared regional genetic background within the Caribbean/American group, although more molecular markers, more populations and specimens are needed to confirm this hypothesis.” (lines 182-184). Also, ”.. indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti. However, given the limited sampling effort, further surveys are needed to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.” (lines 185-188).Also, we changed “...is compatible with a relatively recent arrival on Hispaniola. However, the available data do not allow us to determine the timing or pathway of introduction. Human-mediated transport may have contributed to its spread, but the relative importance of each introduction pathway remains unknown” (lines 190-193).Importantly, we added the sentence: “Additional sampling across Haiti and the use of nuclear and/or genomic markers will be necessary to clarify the distribution, population structure and introduction pathways of the species.” (lines 197-199).Also: “and may provide favorable conditions for the establishment” (line 202), and also: “This potential geographic suitability highlights the possibility of further spread into North America, Central and South America and underscores the value for strengthened surveillance and preparedness beyond the Caribbean.” (lines 215-217).And, finally: “Our findings provide the first confirmed record of Aedes vittatus in Haiti and demonstrate its presence in multiple locations. Further surveillance is needed to determine its distribution, extent of establishment,...” (lines 218-220).Inconsistencies in dates and sites / localities should also be corrected.We have carefully checked and corrected inconsistencies in dates and sampling locations to ensure accuracy and coherence across the manuscript (e.g., sampling period until 31 October 2025 but identifications of Ae. vittatus between 7 and 24 of October). Also the number of localities and municipalities listed in Table I).We have revised in the abstract “Larval surveys were done across 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and North-East departments of Haiti” (Lines 28-29).In Results: “During the sampling period, Ae. vittatus was detected in 8 of 23 sites (34.7%) across..” (lines 137-138).We added also more molecular identifications of other mosquito species, two species that are reported for the first time in Haiti.In the abstract: “Additional mosquito species were identified, including first records of Cx. garciai and Cx. interrogator in Haiti.”In results: “The COI sequencing confirmed the identification of Ps. pygmaea, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus and Cx. interrogator, with the latter showing high similarity to GenBank reference sequences (99.67% identity; MT999299.1). For Culex garciai, no reference sequences are currently available in GenBank; therefore, we generated the first COI sequences for this species in this study.“(lines 178-182).We have also added some clarifications, regarding the molecular work. In material: “...as one of the five samples did not amplify,..” (line107).In the discussion: “Notably, we also reported Cx. garciai and Cx. interrogator from Haiti for the first time. Morphological identification of Cx. interrogator was supported by molecular results, showing high sequence identity but lower query coverage, likely reflecting partial sequences or trimming. (lines 215-218).References are generally relevant and updated, but their formatting should be standardized.We have carefully reviewed and standardized the formatting of all references according to the journal guidelines. The reference list has been thoroughly checked for consistency in authors’ names, journal abbreviations, publication details, page ranges, and DOI formatting. All changes made to the references are indicated in red in the revised manuscript.We believe these revisions have improved the clarity and rigor of the manuscript, and we thank you again for your helpful feedback.Sincerely,David Roiz, in behalf of the authors REVIEWER #1No comments.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to provide evidence of the establishment of Ae. vittatus in Haiti, given its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, and its continued expansion across the Caribbean.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Larval surveys were conducted in 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti, focusing on urban, peri-urban and rural areas during the latter part of the rainy season.
analysis.methods: Mosquito specimens were identified morphologically and confirmed by COI-based DNA barcoding. PCR was performed in duplicate using universal invertebrate-specific primers to amplify a 658-bp fragment of the mitochondrial COI gene, followed by Sanger sequencing and phylogenetic analysis.
analysis.main_results: vittatus was detected in eight of the 23 sites (34.7%) across six municipalities in northern Haiti, with the species found in half of the municipalities sampled.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The detection of Ae. vittatus in one-third of the sampled habitats and half of the surveyed communes, despite limited sampling, indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas, given the potential role of Ae. vittatus as a vector of chikungunya and other arboviruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The limited sampling effort and the absence of Ae. vittatus in earlier surveys in 2013 suggest the need for further studies to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.

analysis.summary_en: This study reports the first detection of the invasive mosquito species Aedes vittatus in Haiti, confirming its presence in eight of 23 sampled sites across six municipalities in the North department. The species was identified through morphological and molecular methods, including COI-based DNA barcoding and phylogenetic analysis. The findings indicate that Ae. vittatus is present in multiple habitats and communes, despite limited sampling, and highlight its potential role as a vector for chikungunya and other arboviruses. The study underscores the importance of continued entomological surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas due to the species' ecological plasticity and dispersal capacity. However, the limited sampling effort and absence from earlier surveys suggest the need for further research to fully understand its distribution and establishment. The evidence is moderate, as the study provides direct detection but lacks broader ecological or epidemiological data.

Key points Chikungunya virus disease should be suspected in patients with acute fever and polyarthralgia and recent travel to an area with chikungunya virus. Several other viruses, including dengue, should be considered in the differential diagnosis depending on travel history and exposures. Rare and serious complications of chikungunya virus disease can occur, particularly among certain risk groups. Disease is usually self-limited, but some patients experience persistent arthralgia for months to years. Clinical presentation Chikungunya virus disease should be considered in patients with acute onset of fever and polyarthralgia, especially travelers who recently returned from areas with known virus transmission. The differential diagnosis varies based on place of residence, travel history, and exposures. Dengue, Zika, and chikungunya viruses are transmitted by the same mosquitoes and have similar clinical features. These viruses can circulate in the same area and can cause occasional co-infections in the same patient. Chikungunya virus infection is more likely to cause high fever, severe arthralgia, arthritis, rash, and lymphopenia, while dengue virus infection is more likely to cause neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, hemorrhage, shock, and death. In general, the signs and symptoms of Zika virus are mild, though infections can cause congenital infections. It is important to rule out dengue virus infection because proper clinical management of dengue can improve outcome. Keep Reading Clinical Features of Dengue In addition to dengue and Zika, other diagnostic considerations include leptospirosis, malaria, rickettsia, group A streptococcus, rubella, measles, parvovirus, enteroviruses, adenovirus, other alphavirus infections (Mayaro, Ross River, Barmah Forest, o’nyong-nyong, and Sindbis viruses), post-infectious arthritis, and rheumatologic conditions. Signs and symptoms The majority of people infected with chikungunya virus become symptomatic. The incubation period is typically 3–7 days (range, 1–12 days). The disease is most often characterized by acute onset of fever (typically >39°C [102°F]) and polyarthralgia. Joint symptoms are usually bilateral and symmetric and can be severe and debilitating. Other symptoms can include headache, myalgia, arthritis, conjunctivitis, nausea/vomiting, or maculopapular rash. Rare complications include uveitis, retinitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, nephritis, bullous skin lesions, hemorrhage, meningoencephalitis, myelitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and cranial nerve palsies. Persons at risk for severe disease include neonates exposed intrapartum or shortly after birth, older adults (>65 years), and persons with underlying medical conditions (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease). Keep Reading Chikungunya Atypical and Severe Disease Manifestations Clinical assessment Clinical laboratory findings can include lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated creatinine. Elevated hepatic transaminases can be seen with acute infection but are not specific and do not occur frequently enough to be diagnostic. Outcomes Acute symptoms typically resolve within 7–10 days. Some patients may have persistence or relapse of rheumatologic symptoms (polyarthralgia, polyarthritis, tenosynovitis) in the months following acute illness. Studies report variable proportions of patients with persistent joint pains for months to years. Mortality is rare and occurs mostly in older adults. analysis.brief_en: The CDC article provides an overview of the clinical signs and symptoms of chikungunya virus disease, emphasizing its acute onset of fever and polyarthralgia, particularly in travelers returning from affected areas. It highlights that joint symptoms are often severe and bilateral, and other symptoms may include headache, myalgia, rash, and lymphopenia. The article also notes that while the disease is usually self-limited, some patients may experience persistent joint pain for months to years. Mortality is rare but more common in older adults. The information is reviewed by subject matter experts as of October 21, 2026, and is based on studies from 2014–2016 and 2019. The article mentions that chikungunya, dengue, and Zika viruses are transmitted by the same mosquitoes and share similar clinical features, but it stresses the importance of differentiating them for proper management. It also notes that complications such as uveitis, myocarditis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome can occur, though they are rare. The content is general and does not report specific outbreaks or case counts, focusing instead on the broader clinical and epidemiological context of the disease.

Close Search & Section Navigation News Features ExclusiveSponsored Opinion Big Interview Guest Blog Awards PB Conference PB Webinar Live RegistrationOn Demand Video Podcast Videos More PB ConferenceLearningGallery Follow us Home> Drug Safety & Medicine Alerts> MHRA withdraws marketing authorisation for IXCHIQ chikungunya vaccine> Submit Guest Post MHRA withdraws marketing authorisation for IXCHIQ chikungunya vaccine The regulator has advised healthcare professionals not to administer the vaccine for individuals travelling to countries with known chikungunya transmission Individuals who have already received the IXCHIQ vaccine do not need another vaccination or any other specific medical treatment because of this decision. Chikungunya By Shajil KumarOct 21, 2026 Shajil Kumar Shajil Kumar is a senior journalist at Pharmacy Business, where he covers daily news, features and investigations and keeps a close eye on the pharmacy sector's biggest stories. With nearly three decades in print and online journalism spanning general and financial news, he brings that depth of experience from his earlier roles at Asian Media Group's sister publications Eastern Eye and India Weekly See Full Bio Key Summary Healthcare professionals should advise travellers of alternative measures to prevent chikungunya infection, including other vaccines. IXCHIQ is a live attenuated vaccine and became available in the UK from June 2025. The UK now has only has one approved chikungunya vaccine - Vimkunya, developed by Bavarian Nordic. The MHRA has withdrawn the marketing authorisation for IXCHIQ chikungunya vaccine following the advice from the Commission on Human Medicines (CHM). The regulator said the benefit-risk balance for the IXCHIQ chikungunya vaccine is no longer favourable and has advised healthcare professionals to consider alternatives. IXCHIQ is a live attenuated vaccine, manufactured by Valneva, and became available in the UK from June 2025. The MHRA has advised healthcare professionals not to prescribe, supply or administer the IXCHIQ vaccine, and dispose of any remaining stock in accordance with local policies. They should advise travellers of alternative measures to prevent chikungunya infection, including other vaccines, avoidance of mosquito bites and adherence to current health-related travel advice. The UK now has only has one approved chikungunya vaccine - Vimkunya, a single-dose vaccine developed by Bavarian Nordic. They should also ensure that any materials, systems or communications referring to available UK vaccination options are updated to remove the IXCHIQ vaccine. Individuals who have already received the IXCHIQ vaccine do not need another vaccination or any other specific medical treatment because of this decision. Those experiencing suspected side effect following the vaccination should seek medical advice. Since the authorisation of IXCHIQ, serious adverse reactions have been reported, including chikungunya-like symptoms and rare neurological events such as encephalitis. Most of these cases involved older adults and individuals with underlying medical conditions were at greater risk. However, some individuals with no known health conditions were also affected. Some cases resulted in hospitalisation or death. After reviewing the post-authorisation safety data and consulting the CHM, the MHRA has decided to withdraw marketing authorisation for the IXCHIQ vaccine. Individuals travelling from the UK to regions with known chikungunya transmission are advised to consider alternative measures. Chikungunya virus is found in the subtropical regions of the Americas, Africa, Southeast Asia, India, and the Pacific Region. The MHRA had on 11 February this year curtailed the usage of IXCHIQ vaccine for adults over the age of 60 years, and all individuals with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, and/or chronic kidney disease. Chikungunya symptoms The chikungunya virus is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Aedes mosquito and the symptoms include sudden onset of fever usually accompanied by joint pain. The joint pain may be very debilitating, but usually ends within a few days or weeks. However, in some cases, joint pain and arthritis may persist for several months or even years. mhracommission on human medicines (chm)ixchiq vaccinecardiovascular diseasechronic kidney diseasediabeteschikungunya vaccine Related News News PRAG unveils plan to boost research in pharmacy Shajil Kumar 1h News Three get jail for £279k fraud at Worcestershire Acute Hospitals NHS Trust Shajil Kumar 2h News CPPE to conduct dermatology workshop for pharmacists, pharmacy technicians Shajil Kumar 6h News RCPharm's Barnett Award for Heather Smith Shajil Kumar 7h

news.content_zh: 药品和保健品监管机构 (MHRA) 已撤销 IXCHIQ 基孔肯雅热 疫苗 的营销授权,自 2026 年 10 月 21 日起生效。这一决定是在对授权后安全数据进行审查并与人类药物委员会 (CHM) 协商后做出的,该委员会得出的结论是,疫苗 的利益-风险平衡不再有利。MHRA 建议医疗保健专业人员不要使用 疫苗 并处置任何剩余库存。他们还应告知旅行者其他预防措施,例如避免蚊虫叮咬和遵循当前的旅行健康建议。据报道,有严重的不良反应,包括基孔肯雅热样症状和脑炎等罕见的神经系统事件,有些病例导致住院或死亡。英国目前只有一种获得批准的基孔肯雅病毒 疫苗,即 Vimkunya,由 Bavarian Nordic 开发。已收到 IXCHIQ 疫苗 的个人无需采取进一步行动,因为不需要额外的医疗 治疗。MHRA 还敦促更新所有材料和系统,以删除对 IXCHIQ 疫苗 的引用。

news.title: Honduras Confirms Local Chikungunya Spread
news.excerpt: Honduras confirmed eight chikungunya cases and local spread near the Nicaraguan border. What it is, what the CDC says and what travellers should know.

news.content: A US Navy preventive-medicine officer marks the location of every house in the Monte Verde area of Choloma, Honduras, so an aid group can track mosquito control during the 2016 Zika response. File photo from 17 August 2016, not from the current outbreak. (Photo: US Navy Combat Camera, Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Torrey W. Lee, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons) HONDURAS · HEALTH · MOSQUITO-BORNE VIRUS Honduras’s health ministry has confirmed eight cases of chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus that causes severe joint pain, including a cluster that is spreading locally in a border village near Nicaragua. Key Facts — The count Eight lab-confirmed cases: four in the capital district, two in Atlántida, one each in El Paraíso and Olancho. — The cluster Local spread in El Pedregalito, Alauca, about 5 km (3 miles) from the Nicaraguan border. — First import A 31-year-old trucker back from Managua was the first imported case of 2026, confirmed Friday 4 September. — The US link Neighbouring Nicaragua carries a Level 2 US health notice for chikungunya, updated 3 September. — Still open How many people are sick in the border village is not public. Honduras’s health ministry has confirmed eight cases of chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus that causes severe joint pain, and says the virus is now spreading between people inside the country. The cluster is in El Pedregalito, a village in the municipality of Alauca about 5 kilometres (3 miles) from the Nicaraguan border, Homer Mejía, the ministry’s head of health surveillance, said on Friday 23 October. For US readers the news matters because chikungunya can be caught on trips to Central America, and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) already lists a Level 2 travel health notice for neighbouring Nicaragua. The CDC’s notices page listed no chikungunya notice for Honduras on Sunday morning, 25 October. In Plain English Chikungunya: a viral disease spread by Aedes mosquitoes that causes fever and severe joint pain. Deaths are rare, according to the CDC. a viral disease spread by Aedes mosquitoes that causes fever and severe joint pain. Deaths are rare, according to the CDC. Local (community) spread: people are being infected inside Honduras by local mosquitoes, not only after trips abroad. people are being infected inside Honduras by local mosquitoes, not only after trips abroad. Sesal: Honduras’s Secretaría de Salud, the health ministry that runs public hospitals and tracks disease outbreaks. Honduras’s Secretaría de Salud, the health ministry that runs public hospitals and tracks disease outbreaks. elements_zh.location_and_population: 暴发 事件发生在洪都拉斯阿劳卡市的一个村庄埃尔佩德雷加利托,靠近尼加拉瓜边境。受影响人口包括边境村庄和首都地区、亚特兰蒂达、埃尔帕拉伊索和奥兰乔的居民。该病毒由伊蚊传播。
elements_zh.event: 洪都拉斯卫生部确认了八例经实验室确诊的基孔肯雅热病例,其中包括阿劳卡州埃尔佩德雷加利托的本地传播群。首例输入病例是一名从尼加拉瓜马那瓜回国的31岁卡车司机。该部报告了该国当地的 传播,在边境村庄的家庭中发现了症状。

analysis_zh.event: 洪都拉斯卫生部确认了八例经实验室确诊的基孔肯雅热病例,其中包括阿劳卡州埃尔佩德雷加利托的本地传播群。首例输入病例是一名从尼加拉瓜马那瓜回国的31岁卡车司机。该部报告了该国当地的 传播,在边境村庄的家庭中发现了症状。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, October 22, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Blood samples showed longer chikungunya detection in hospitalized patients by October 22, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Blood samples showed longer chikungunya detection in hospitalized patients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Blood samples detected chikungunya virus more consistently and for longer than saliva or urine in a longitudinal study of 53 hospitalized patients in Nanning, China, during the country’s largest recorded chikungunya outbreak in 2025. Researchers collected 506 body-fluid specimens and found that serum and plasma were positive in most samples, whereas positivity was substantially lower in saliva and urine. The findings indicate that blood was the more informative specimen type for assessing detection during acute illness, although the results are limited to a hospitalized cohort and should not automatically be applied to people with mild or asymptomatic infection. Chikungunya virus is an acute mosquito-borne infection transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. The study followed hospitalized patients with symptomatic disease and compared the probability of positive test results in serum, plasma, saliva and urine at different points after symptom onset. Serum had the highest observed positivity rate, at 81.20%, followed by plasma at 72.50%. Saliva was positive in 11.03% of samples and urine in 4.73%. Discover more Find Treatments Study Anatomy Biology textbook sales Investigators also compared cycle-threshold, or Ct, values between specimen types. During the first four days after symptoms began, median Ct values were lower in serum and plasma than in saliva and urine. The analysis therefore found stronger and more consistent detection in blood specimens early in illness. The study used these laboratory values to compare the timing of detection across specimen types; it did not use them to establish how much infectious virus was present in any sample. Discover more Check Symptoms Get Health Tips Study Biology Book Lab Tests A generalized estimating equations model was used to estimate how the probability of a positive result changed with the number of days since symptom onset. The sharpest decline occurred in saliva: its estimated probability of testing positive fell from 52.2% on day 1 to 0.7% by day 7. Blood positivity declined more gradually. Serum and plasma positivity rates were both above 85% on day 3 and were approximately 30% by day 7. Urine remained at a low positivity level throughout, and the number of days since symptom onset was not significantly associated with a positive urine result. These are modeled probabilities based on the study’s observed specimens, rather than measurements of infectious virus or proof that a person remained contagious for the same duration. The models also describe the study population and sampling schedule, so the day-specific estimates should not be interpreted as universal values for every patient or every specimen collection method. The relatively low number of positive urine samples further limited the precision of conclusions about that fluid. Parametric survival analysis provided additional estimates of the duration of detection. The median duration was 5.8 days in serum, with a 95% confidence interval of 4.8 to 6.9 days, and also 5.8 days in plasma, with a 95% confidence interval of 4.7 to 7.1 days. Saliva had a shorter median detection period of 3.5 days, with a 95% confidence interval of 3.0 to 4.1 days. Urine was excluded from this analysis because too few urine samples tested positive to support the model. Taken together, the results show that blood specimens retained detectable chikungunya virus longer and with greater consistency than the non-blood fluids examined. Saliva performed better than urine for detecting the virus during the acute phase, but its modeled positivity fell quickly. The findings support blood as the preferred sample type for detecting chikungunya virus and estimating how long detection persisted in the body during the period studied. They do not establish the duration of viable virus, whether transmission could occur from any specimen, or whether the same patterns occur outside hospitalized patients. Discover more Book Care Services Read Med Journals infections infection infectious The study was conducted in a single city during the 2025 outbreak, and its hospitalized population may not represent the wider range of chikungunya infections. Repeated specimens were available for 53 patients, but the analysis was limited to the body-fluid samples collected from that cohort and to the laboratory tests performed. Within those limits, the results provide a specimen-focused account of chikungunya detection dynamics during acute disease and identify differences between blood, saliva and urine that may help frame subsequent surveillance and public health control work. news.title_zh: 血液样本显示住院患者的基孔肯雅热检测时间更长 - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: A study in Nanning, China, found that blood samples detected chikungunya virus more consistently and for longer than saliva or urine in hospitalized patients during the 2025 outbreak. Serum and plasma had the highest positivity rates, while saliva and urine showed lower rates. This supports blood as the preferred sample type for detecting chikungunya virus and estimating its persistence in the body.
news.content_zh: 中国南宁的一项研究发现,在 2025 年 暴发 期间,住院患者的血液样本检测到 基孔肯雅病毒 的一致性比唾液或尿液的 基孔肯雅病毒 的检测结果更一致,持续时间也更长。血清和血浆的阳性率最高,而唾液和尿液的阳性率较低。这支持血液作为检测 基孔肯雅病毒 并估计其在体内持久性的首选样本类型。

Dismiss Opt out Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information Regulatory Update 1 min read UK revokes Valneva's chikungunya vaccine marketing approval Earlier this year, Valneva voluntarily withdrew the vaccine from the US market following a safety investigation launched by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the wake of several serious adverse events. Online Bureau ET Pharma Updated On Oct 22, 2026 at 05:58 PM IST London: The UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has ordered the "withdrawal of the marketing authorisation" of Valneva’s chikungunya vaccine, Ixchiq. Following a post-authorisation safety review and suggestion by the Commission on Human Medicines, the UK’s medicines regulator said the benefit-risk balance of the vaccine was no longer considered favourable. Healthcare professionals have been prohibited from prescribing or administering the vaccine. Advt Patients who have previously received Ixchiq have been advised to take medical advice if they have experienced a suspected adverse reaction following vaccination. Ixchiq is single-dose live attenuated vaccine indicated for the prevention of chikungunya virus infection in adults travelling to high-risk areas. Since its authorisation, MHRA flagged that, "serious adverse reactions have been reported, including chikungunya-like symptoms and rare neurological events such as encephalitis." Event Biotech Leadership Symposium 2026 India’s biotech industry, has largely been driven by vaccines, biosimilars and contract manufacturing. The country already supplies over 60 per cent of global vaccines, reinforcing its reputation as a global manufacturing powerhouse. However, the next decade will be defined by more complex scientific challenges: vaccines for emerging pathogens, therapies for rare diseases affecting an estimated 70 to 96 million Indians, and solutions to antimicrobial resistance (AMR), which contributes to over 1 million deaths annually in India. As Indian companies begin investing in mRNA platforms, cell and gene therapies, and advanced biologics, the critical question is whether India can transition from scale and supply to discovery-driven global biotech leadership. Fri, 11 Dec 2026 Le Meridien, Hyderabad Register Now 10 Speakers Event RE-Pharma Summit 2027 India’s pharmaceutical industry having cemented its position as the “pharmacy of the world” through decades of dominance in generics, the time has come to ask some hard questions: Can India ever match global innovation prowess? Or are we too entrenched in concentrating on generics and cost arbitrage to make that leap? Fri, 12 Feb 2027 Sahara Star, Mumbai Register Now Award RE-Pharma Awards 2027 Pharma is no longer defined only by what is manufactured and prescribed. It is increasingly shaped by what is discovered, how quickly it moves from research to reality, and how effectively innovation reaches the people who need it. Fri, 12 Feb 2027 Know More Show More Most reported cases involved older adults, including those without pre-existing medical conditions. Some cases resulted in hospitalisation or death. The MHRA has directed French vaccine maker to recall all batches of the vaccine from the market. Ixchiq accounts for nearly 5 per ent of Valneva’s net sales and was the world’s first vaccine approved against chikungunya. However, its safety profile has remained under regulatory scrutiny. Advt Earlier this year, Valneva voluntarily withdrew the vaccine from the US market following a safety investigation launched by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the wake of several serious adverse events. Ixchiq competes with Bavarian Nordic’s Vimkunya, which uses non-infectious virus-like particles (VLPs) to trigger an immune response. In contrast, Valneva’s vaccine carries a modified strain of the chikungunya virus to develop immune response. analysis.event: The UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) revoked Valneva's marketing authorization for its chikungunya vaccine, Ixchiq, due to safety concerns following a post-authorisation safety review.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The vaccine was indicated for adults travelling to high-risk areas. Serious adverse reactions, including chikungunya-like symptoms and rare neurological events such as encephalitis, were reported. Some cases resulted in hospitalisation or death.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Healthcare professionals have been prohibited from prescribing or administering the vaccine. Patients who have received Ixchiq are advised to seek medical advice if they experience suspected adverse reactions. The vaccine will be recalled from the market.

On this day,1972, DDT, the first of the modern insecticides used against malaria and typhus, is banned by the United States Environmental Protection Agency after evidence of adverse environmental side effects.(Photo: Pixabay) Latest News , News October 22, 2026 PAHO urges Caribbean to prepare for dengue, chikungunya rise Loading Audio Player By Instaread, Please Wait... WASHINGTON, United States (CMC) – The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) is urging Caribbean countries to strengthen disease surveillance and prepare health services for possible increases in dengue and chikungunya, amid renewed transmission in parts of the Americas and the anticipated intensification of the El Niño phenomenon. In an epidemiological update issued on Wednesday, PAHO reported 1.69 million suspected dengue cases across the Americas as of mid-September, including 3,413 severe cases and 571 deaths. Sports Antonelli storms to US Grand Prix pole on weekend he can take title October 25, 2026 AUSTIN, Texas (AFP) — Runaway world championship leader Kimi Antonelli showed no nerves as he stormed to pole position with a perfectly measured faste... {"xml":"xml"} {"jamaica-observer":"Jamaica Observer"} Although the cumulative number of reported cases was 58 per cent lower than during the same period in 2025, the agency said the decline had not been consistent across the region. Increases had been observed in recent weeks in the Andean, Central American and Caribbean subregions, while all four dengue virus serotypes were circulating in the Americas in 2026. Football, Sports Arteta hails mentality as Arsenal go level with Man City October 25, 2026 LONDON, England (AFP) — Mikel Arteta praised the mentality of centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel Magalhaes after they both scored in a 2-0 win that t... {"xml":"xml"} {"jamaica-observer":"Jamaica Observer"} PAHO also raised concerns about chikungunya, reporting increased transmission between late 2025 and 2026, including renewed circulation in countries and territories where the virus had not been detected for several years. As of mid-September, 213,919 suspected chikungunya cases had been reported across 20 countries in the region. Of these, 78,481 were confirmed, with 88 deaths recorded. Football, Sports COULD IT BE? Reggae Girlz superstar Shaw on brink of history with women’s Ballon d’Or in sight October 26, 2026 Khadija “Bunny” Shaw stands on the verge of history today, with the Reggae Girlz captain in contention to become the first Jamaican to claim football’... {"xml":"xml"} {"jamaica-observer":"Jamaica Observer"} The agency also pointed to transmission in new areas, outbreaks outside historically affected seasons, longer periods of transmission and increased reports of more severe clinical manifestations. PAHO is calling on countries to strengthen epidemiological, virological and entomological surveillance, expand diagnostic capacity and ensure that cases are detected early and patients receive timely care. It also recommended stronger integrated measures to control Aedes mosquitoes, which transmit both diseases. Health services should be prepared to respond to potential increases in cases at all levels of care, PAHO said, with particular attention to strengthening primary healthcare workers’ ability to recognise dengue warning signs early and prevent progression to severe illness. Hospitals should also be ready to manage patients with warning signs and severe cases, the agency added. PAHO further urged countries to improve environmental management, remove containers that collect water and encourage communities, families, local authorities and other sectors to participate actively in mosquito prevention and control. Eliminating mosquito breeding sites remains a key measure in reducing mosquito populations, the agency said. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 24, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Persistent symptoms common after Ebola and chikungunya across Africa, review finds by October 24, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Persistent symptoms common after Ebola and chikungunya across Africa, review finds Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Survivors of Ebola virus disease and chikungunya across Africa frequently experience persistent symptoms lasting weeks to years after their acute infection, according to a systematic review published in BMC Infectious Diseases. The review examined post-acute infection syndromes following non-COVID infections, a family of conditions that has gained global attention through long COVID. Although many pathogens most closely linked to these syndromes are endemic to Africa, evidence from the continent has remained scarce. The peer-reviewed article is being shared early to provide faster access and will be replaced by the final Version of Record. Researchers searched Medline, Embase and grey literature up to 7 November 2025 for studies conducted in Africa that reported symptoms four or more weeks after acute infection. Case reports, case series, conference abstracts, secondary research, comments and correspondence were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened the records and extracted data on study characteristics, symptom prevalence, clinical presentation and associated factors. Because substantial heterogeneity was observed across the included studies, the findings were summarised descriptively rather than pooled statistically, and the review was registered on the Open Science Framework. Of 1,368 records, 65 studies were included, most carrying a moderate to low risk of bias. Forty-two studies examined Ebola virus disease and 19 examined chikungunya. The authors describe the evidence base as scarce, heterogeneous and geographically concentrated, and note that many pathogens most closely linked to post-acute infection syndromes are endemic to Africa, a gap they frame as having implications for both health equity and global health security. Discover more Check Symptoms Study Biology Track Outbreaks Infectious Diseases infections Prevalence estimates varied widely. Between 17.5 percent and 98.6 percent of Ebola survivors reported persistent symptoms, while the range after chikungunya stretched from 12.1 percent to 78.6 percent. The authors refrained from combining these estimates into a single headline prevalence, summarising the results descriptively in view of the substantial heterogeneity across studies. Despite the spread of figures, the reported prevalence of persistent symptoms among survivors was high. The clinical picture differed between the two diseases. After Ebola, musculoskeletal pain, ocular complications, headache and fatigue predominated. After chikungunya, arthralgia was the hallmark of post-chikungunya disease. Across the included studies, a substantial symptom burden persisted years after the acute infection. Across studies, three factors emerged most frequently as being associated with persistent sequelae: female sex, older age and greater severity of the acute illness. The review reports these as the factors most frequently associated with persistent sequelae in the included studies, not as proven causes of persistent illness. An exploratory, non-systematic supplementary search additionally identified sex-specific consequences among female survivors, including menstrual irregularities and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Because this supplementary component was not conducted systematically, the authors present it as a signal for future targeted research rather than a firm estimate of how commonly these reproductive health complications occur. Discover more infection Find Treatments Health health Get Health Tips The review also highlights a fundamental interpretive limitation: most included studies lacked comparison groups. The authors caution that the absence of comparison groups in most studies complicates attribution of the persistent symptoms to the infection itself. The high reported prevalence is therefore best understood as a measure of the documented symptom burden among survivors rather than a definitive causal estimate. Despite these caveats, the authors argue that the implications for health systems are clear. Health systems in Africa must adapt to provide long-term survivor care, embedding follow-up into existing chronic care platforms. As pathogens endemic to the continent carry pandemic potential and expand geographically, the review concludes that understanding their chronic consequences is both a matter of health equity and an urgent global health security priority. news.content_zh: 2026 年《BMC 传染病》杂志上发表的一项系统综述发现,非洲各地的埃博拉病毒病和基孔肯雅热幸存者在急性感染后经常会出现持续数周至数年的持续症状。该综述分析了截至 2025 年 11 月 7 日的研究,确定了广泛的 患病率 估计值,基孔肯雅热为 12.1% 至 78.6%,埃博拉为 17.5% 至 98.6%。持续症状包括肌肉骨骼疼痛、眼部并发症、头痛、疲劳和 关节痛。作者强调了非洲对幸存者进行长期护理和调整卫生系统的必要性,并指出大多数研究中缺乏比较组,使明确的因果归因变得复杂。他们还强调了了解这些对健康公平和全球卫生安全的长期后果的重要性。

news.content_title: One mosquito and the look-alike fevers that arrive with the rains
news.content: Health One mosquito and the look-alike fevers that arrive with the rains Dengue, chikungunya and Zika are spread by the same mosquito and share similar symptoms in the early days. Here’s how to tell them apart, why a blood test is needed to confirm the infection, and which warning signs warrant an immediate hospital visit. When the rains arrive and water collects in pots, tyres and terraces, so do the mosquitoes. For many families in monsoon-hit cities like Chennai, the first sign of trouble is a fever that comes with body aches and a headache, and the first question is whether it’s dengue, chikungunya or something else. That is a fair question, because all three are spread by the same mosquito and can look almost identical in the first few days. We spoke to doctors about the clues that help tell them apart, why only a blood test can settle it, what to do at home, and the warning signs that mean heading to the hospital the same day. Why they are so hard to tell apart During seasons when mosquito-borne infections are prevalent, dengue, chikungunya and Zika can be difficult to distinguish because they often begin with similar symptoms, including fever, headache, muscle pain and body aches. However, according to Dr. Tushar Tayal, Associate Director, Internal Medicine, CK Birla Hospital, Gurugram, certain clinical features can help doctors identify the likely infection. Early days can be tricky. “Difference between Chikungunya and Zika in the first two days is hard to tell. Both Chikungunya and Zika come from the Aedes mosquito, the same one that spreads Dengue,” says Dr. Sushila Kataria, Vice Chairperson, Internal Medicine, Medanta Gurugram. “Dengue, chikungunya and Zika can look alike in the first few days, but Dengue is the one I worry about most, because platelets can drop quickly,” she adds. Dengue: severe body aches and falling platelets “Dengue may present with severe body aches, pain behind the eyes, a falling platelet count and, in some cases, warning signs such as abdominal pain, persistent vomiting or bleeding,” Dr. Tayal says. “Early assessment is particularly important in suspected Dengue, as the risk of complications can increase around the time the fever begins to settle,” he cautions. Chikungunya: the joints give it away “With chikungunya, the joints give it away,” says Dr. Kataria. “The fever comes on suddenly and is usually quite high, and then the pain sets in, mostly in the wrists, fingers, knees and ankles,” she explains. “Patients tell me they can’t open a bottle or climb stairs. In some people the stiffness stays for weeks after the fever is gone,” Dr. Kataria says. Dr. Tayal describes it in similar terms. “Chikungunya is more commonly associated with intense joint pain, swelling and stiffness, which may persist for weeks or even months after the fever subsides,” he says. Zika: usually mild, but not for everyone “Zika infection is often milder and may cause a characteristic rash, red eyes and joint pain, although many infected individuals experience few or no symptoms,” Dr. Tayal says. “Most people barely have symptoms while others may get a mild fever, red eyes and an itchy rash,” says Dr. Kataria. “But if a woman is pregnant, it needs to be taken seriously, because the virus can affect the baby’s brain. Any pregnant woman with fever and rash should get tested without waiting,” she cautions. Only a blood test can tell you which one it is The key is not to rely on symptoms alone. “A patient’s travel history, local outbreak patterns, day of illness and clinical examination all guide the diagnostic approach,” Dr. Tayal explains, adding that laboratory tests, including appropriate molecular or antibody tests depending on the stage of infection, help confirm the diagnosis. “Since the symptoms overlap, doctors rely on timing, symptom patterns and blood tests rather than guesswork,” Dr. Kataria says, advising that it is not a safe thing to guess which of the three one has, getting a blood test is. What to do at home According to the experts, drink plenty of fluids, and avoid painkillers like ibuprofen unless your doctor says so. Patients should avoid self-medication, particularly aspirin and ibuprofen until dengue has been ruled out, as these medicines can increase the risk of bleeding. Timely diagnosis and appropriate monitoring are essential to prevent complications and ensure effective management. When to head to the hospital the same day “If there’s bleeding, constant vomiting or severe stomach pain, go to the hospital the same day,” Dr. Kataria says. Dengue, chikungunya and Zika may look alike at the start, but one doesn’t have to stay clueless. If a fever and body aches show up during the rains, don’t wait it out or guess. Get a blood test, drink plenty of fluids and skip painkillers like ibuprofen unless your doctor says so. And if there is bleeding, constant vomiting or severe stomach pain, head to the hospital the same day. The New Indian Express www.newindianexpress.com

微信 腾讯QQ QQ空间 (来源:白沙融媒) 所谓“蚊媒传染病”,就是蚊子在叮咬时把病毒或寄生虫“快递”到人体内的疾病;国内需要重点盯防的有登革热、基孔肯雅热、寨卡病毒病、乙型脑炎和疟疾等。 今天,我们先锁定由伊蚊“投递”的两大热门疾病——登革热与基孔肯雅热。 01 什么是登革热? 它是由登革病毒引起的,经伊蚊叮咬传播的虫媒传染病。据世界卫生组织统计,全球每年约有1-4亿人感染,其中美洲、东南亚和西太平洋(3.350, 0.00, 0.00%)区域发病最为严重,亚洲约占全球疾病负担的70%。我国广东、云南、广西等多个省份曾多次发生本地疫情。 02 登革热的典型症状有哪些? 登革热的潜伏期(从被携带病毒的蚊子叮咬到症状开始的时间)一般为1-14天,多为5-9天。值得注意的是大多数感染者没有症状或症状轻微,不过,一旦发病,患者会出现一系列典型症状: 1.突发高热:体温可达40°C以上; 2.“三痛”:剧烈头痛、眼眶痛、全身肌肉关节痛; 3.“三红”:面部、颈部、胸部潮红; 4.皮疹:四肢或躯干出现充血性红疹; 5.消化道症状:恶心、呕吐、腹泻、食欲不振等消化道症状; 6.严重者:可发展为登革出血热或登革休克综合征,甚至危及生命。 03 什么是基孔肯雅热? 基孔肯雅热(Chikungunya fever)是一种由基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)引起,通过白纹伊蚊或埃及伊蚊传播的病毒性疾病。基孔肯雅热始发于非洲,最早于1952年在坦桑尼亚首次被发现。“基孔肯雅”一词就来源于坦桑尼亚南部基马孔德语,意思是“变得扭曲”,用以描述出现严重关节疼痛的感染者痛得弯腰、蜷缩身体的样子。 根据世界卫生组织公布的最新数据,截至2024年12月,全球119个国家和地区已报告基孔肯雅热本地传播。 近些年我国周边的东南亚疫情持续活跃。我国于2008年首次发现输入性病例,曾引发本地疫情,但尚未形成稳定的疫源地。2025年7月广东省佛山市发生疫情,经全力防控,现疫情已呈明显下降趋势。 04 基孔肯雅热有何症状? 被带基孔肯雅病毒的蚊子叮咬后,病毒在体内潜伏期通常为3-7天(最短1天,最长可达12天),随后可能突然发病,出现典型的“热-疹-痛”三联征: 🔺 突发高烧:体温可高达39°C以上,可能持续1-7天。部分患者会出现“双峰热”,即退烧后再次发热。 🔺 皮疹:约80%的患者在发热后2-5天,面部、四肢甚至手掌脚底会出现红色斑疹或丘疹,常伴有瘙痒。 🔺 明显关节疼痛:这是基孔肯雅热最突出的特点之一。特别是手指、手腕、脚踝和脚趾等小关节会出现剧烈疼痛和肿胀,可能持续数天甚至数月。 此外,还可能伴随头痛、恶心、呕吐、肌肉痛、结膜炎等症状。 05 这两种疾病有什么区别? 这两种疾病,各年龄人群普遍易感,发病初期都会出现高热、头痛、关节和肌肉疼痛等症状。 登革热发生重症的比例较高,致死病例时有发生。基孔肯雅热多数患者为轻症,大约会在1~2周内康复,但部分人(尤其是老年人和慢性病患者)可能会经历长期关节疼痛的折磨;只有极少数情况下,该病会导致出血、脑炎等严重并发症甚至死亡。 两种疾病的特征对比 在登革热和基孔肯雅热共同流行的地区,常有人同时感染两种病毒。 06 这两种疾病是如何传播的? 登革热和基孔肯雅热的传播途径相似,都是由白纹伊蚊和埃及伊蚊传播。伊蚊白天叮咬人,尤其活跃于日出后1-2小时和日落前2-3小时。它们的幼虫孳生于小型积水容器中,如瓶罐、废旧轮胎、花盆等,这些地方都可能成为它们的“温床”。 07 如何预防这两种疾病? 面对蚊媒传染病的威胁,我们可以通过科学有效的预防措施,降低被其感染的风险: 1.环境治理:伊蚊依赖小型积水繁殖,因此清除蚊虫孳生地是预防虫媒传染病的根本措施。我们需要定时清理家中容易积水的地方,如瓶罐、废旧轮胎、花盆、下水道、杂物堆等区域,不给蚊子提供繁殖的机会。 2.个人防护:外出时,尽量穿浅色长袖衣裤,减少皮肤暴露面积;同时在裸露皮肤上涂抹含避蚊胺、避蚊酯的驱蚊液。在家中,安装纱门纱窗,使用蚊帐,为自己打造一个安全的“无蚊空间”;必要时使用电蚊拍、灭蚊灯等,对蚊子进行“精准打击”。此外,尽量减少在户外树阴、草丛等蚊子多的地方逗留时间。 3.关注流行区疫情:如果计划前往东南亚、非洲等登革热和基孔肯雅热流行区,出行前一定要查询当地疫情信息,做好充分的驱蚊防蚊准备。归国后14天内做好健康监测,密切关注自己的身体状况。 4.及时就医:一旦出现发热、皮疹、关节痛等相关症状立即就医并告知旅行史和蚊虫叮咬史,以便医生能够及时准确地诊断和治疗。 海量资讯、精准解读,尽在新浪财经APP 微博 分享 MD 微信 腾讯QQ QQ空间 (来源:白沙融媒) 所谓“蚊媒传染病”,就是蚊子在叮咬时把病毒或寄生虫“快递”到人体内的疾病;国内需要重点盯防的有登革热、基孔肯雅热、寨卡病毒病、乙型脑炎和疟疾等。 今天,我们先锁定由伊蚊“投递”的两大热门疾病——登革热与基孔肯雅热。 01 什么是登革热? 它是由登革病毒引起的,经伊蚊叮咬传播的虫媒传染病。据世界卫生组织统计,全球每年约有1-4亿人感染,其中美洲、东南亚和西太平洋(3.350, 0.00, 0.00%)区域发病最为严重,亚洲约占全球疾病负担的70%。我国广东、云南、广西等多个省份曾多次发生本地疫情。 02 登革热的典型症状有哪些? 登革热的潜伏期(从被携带病毒的蚊子叮咬到症状开始的时间)一般为1-14天,多为5-9天。值得注意的是大多数感染者没有症状或症状轻微,不过,一旦发病,患者会出现一系列典型症状: 1.突发高热:体温可达40°C以上; 2.“三痛”:剧烈头痛、眼眶痛、全身肌肉关节痛; 3.“三红”:面部、颈部、胸部潮红; 4.皮疹:四肢或躯干出现充血性红疹; 5.消化道症状:恶心、呕吐、腹泻、食欲不振等消化道症状; 6.严重者:可发展为登革出血热或登革休克综合征,甚至危及生命。 03 什么是基孔肯雅热? 基孔肯雅热(Chikungunya fever)是一种由基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)引起,通过白纹伊蚊或埃及伊蚊传播的病毒性疾病。基孔肯雅热始发于非洲,最早于1952年在坦桑尼亚首次被发现。“基孔肯雅”一词就来源于坦桑尼亚南部基马孔德语,意思是“变得扭曲”,用以描述出现严重关节疼痛的感染者痛得弯腰、蜷缩身体的样子。 根据世界卫生组织公布的最新数据,截至2024年12月,全球119个国家和地区已报告基孔肯雅热本地传播。 近些年我国周边的东南亚疫情持续活跃。我国于2008年首次发现输入性病例,曾引发本地疫情,但尚未形成稳定的疫源地。2025年7月广东省佛山市发生疫情,经全力防控,现疫情已呈明显下降趋势。 04 基孔肯雅热有何症状? 被带基孔肯雅病毒的蚊子叮咬后,病毒在体内潜伏期通常为3-7天(最短1天,最长可达12天),随后可能突然发病,出现典型的“热-疹-痛”三联征: 🔺 突发高烧:体温可高达39°C以上,可能持续1-7天。部分患者会出现“双峰热”,即退烧后再次发热。 🔺 皮疹:约80%的患者在发热后2-5天,面部、四肢甚至手掌脚底会出现红色斑疹或丘疹,常伴有瘙痒。 🔺 明显关节疼痛:这是基孔肯雅热最突出的特点之一。特别是手指、手腕、脚踝和脚趾等小关节会出现剧烈疼痛和肿胀,可能持续数天甚至数月。 此外,还可能伴随头痛、恶心、呕吐、肌肉痛、结膜炎等症状。 05 这两种疾病有什么区别? 这两种疾病,各年龄人群普遍易感,发病初期都会出现高热、头痛、关节和肌肉疼痛等症状。 登革热发生重症的比例较高,致死病例时有发生。基孔肯雅热多数患者为轻症,大约会在1~2周内康复,但部分人(尤其是老年人和慢性病患者)可能会经历长期关节疼痛的折磨;只有极少数情况下,该病会导致出血、脑炎等严重并发症甚至死亡。 两种疾病的特征对比 在登革热和基孔肯雅热共同流行的地区,常有人同时感染两种病毒。 06 这两种疾病是如何传播的? 登革热和基孔肯雅热的传播途径相似,都是由白纹伊蚊和埃及伊蚊传播。伊蚊白天叮咬人,尤其活跃于日出后1-2小时和日落前2-3小时。它们的幼虫孳生于小型积水容器中,如瓶罐、废旧轮胎、花盆等,这些地方都可能成为它们的“温床”。 07 如何预防这两种疾病? 面对蚊媒传染病的威胁,我们可以通过科学有效的预防措施,降低被其感染的风险: 1.环境治理:伊蚊依赖小型积水繁殖,因此清除蚊虫孳生地是预防虫媒传染病的根本措施。我们需要定时清理家中容易积水的地方,如瓶罐、废旧轮胎、花盆、下水道、杂物堆等区域,不给蚊子提供繁殖的机会。 2.个人防护:外出时,尽量穿浅色长袖衣裤,减少皮肤暴露面积;同时在裸露皮肤上涂抹含避蚊胺、避蚊酯的驱蚊液。在家中,安装纱门纱窗,使用蚊帐,为自己打造一个安全的“无蚊空间”;必要时使用电蚊拍、灭蚊灯等,对蚊子进行“精准打击”。此外,尽量减少在户外树阴、草丛等蚊子多的地方逗留时间。 source_language_evidence.brief_en: 新浪首页 新闻 体育 财经 娱乐 科技 博客 图片 专栏 更多 汽车 教育 时尚 女性 星座 健康 房产历史视频收藏育儿读书 佛学游戏旅游邮箱导航 移动客户端 新浪微博 新浪新闻 新浪财经 新浪体育 新浪众测 新浪博客 新浪视频 新浪游戏 天气通 我的收藏 注册 登录 × 新浪微博、博客、邮箱帐号,请直接登录 加载中。换个账号登录 × 登录 下次自动登录 忘记密码立即注册 使用QQ登录 请用最新版微博客户端扫码 扫描成功! 点击手机上的确认即可登录 自媒体热点 > 正文 行情 股吧 新闻 外汇 新三板 行情 行情 股吧 新闻 外汇 新三板 登革热VS基孔肯雅热:症状对比、传播途径和预防措施 登革热VS基孔肯雅热:症状对比、传播途径和预防措施 2026年10月26日 10:44 市场资讯 新浪财经APP举报 缩小字体 放大字体 收藏 微博 分享 MD 微信 腾讯QQ QQ空间 (来源:白沙融媒) 所谓“蚊媒传染病”,就是蚊子在叮咬时把病毒或寄生虫“快递”到人体内的疾病;国内需要重点盯防的有登革热、基孔肯雅热、寨卡病毒病、乙型脑炎和疟疾等。 今天,我们先锁定由伊蚊“投递”的两大热门疾病——登革热与基孔肯雅热。 它是由登革病毒引起的,经伊蚊叮咬传播的虫媒传染病。据世界卫生组织统计,全球每年约有1-4亿人感染,其中美洲、东南亚和西太平洋(3.350, 0.00, 0.00%)区域发病最为严重,亚洲约占全球疾病负担的70%。我国广东、云南、广西等多个省份曾多次发生本地疫情。 登革热的潜伏期(从被携带病毒的蚊子叮咬到症状开始的时间)一般为1-14天,多为5-9天。值得注意的是大多数感染者没有症状或症状轻微,不过,一旦发病,患者会出现一系列典型症状: 1.突发高热:体温可达40°C以上; 2.“三痛”:剧烈头痛、眼眶痛、全身肌肉关节痛; 3.“三红”:面部、颈部、胸部潮红; 4.皮疹:四肢或躯干出现充血性红疹; 5.消化道症状:恶心、呕吐、腹泻、食欲不振等消化道症状; 6.严重者:可发展为登革出血热或登革休克综合征,甚至危及生命。 基孔肯雅热(Chikungunya fever)是一种由基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)引起,通过白纹伊蚊或埃及伊蚊传播的病毒性疾病。基孔肯雅热始发于非洲,最早于1952年在坦桑尼亚首次被发现。“基孔肯雅”一词就来源于坦桑尼亚南部基马孔德语,意思是“变得扭曲”,用以描述出现严重关节疼痛的感染者痛得弯腰、蜷缩身体的样子。 根据世界卫生组织公布的最新数据,截至2024年12月,全球119个国家和地区已报告基孔肯雅热本地传播。

supplementary_news.content_title: Blood samples showed longer chikungunya detection in hospitalized patients
supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, October 22, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Blood samples showed longer chikungunya detection in hospitalized patients by October 22, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Blood samples showed longer chikungunya detection in hospitalized patients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Blood samples detected chikungunya virus more consistently and for longer than saliva or urine in a longitudinal study of 53 hospitalized patients in Nanning, China, during the country’s largest recorded chikungunya outbreak in 2025. Researchers collected 506 body-fluid specimens and found that serum and plasma were positive in most samples, whereas positivity was substantially lower in saliva and urine. The findings indicate that blood was the more informative specimen type for assessing detection during acute illness, although the results are limited to a hospitalized cohort and should not automatically be applied to people with mild or asymptomatic infection. Chikungunya virus is an acute mosquito-borne infection transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. The study followed hospitalized patients with symptomatic disease and compared the probability of positive test results in serum, plasma, saliva and urine at different points after symptom onset. Serum had the highest observed positivity rate, at 81.20%, followed by plasma at 72.50%. Saliva was positive in 11.03% of samples and urine in 4.73%. Investigators also compared cycle-threshold, or Ct, values between specimen types. During the first four days after symptoms began, median Ct values were lower in serum and plasma than in saliva and urine. The analysis therefore found stronger and more consistent detection in blood specimens early in illness. The study used these laboratory values to compare the timing of detection across specimen types; it did not use them to establish how much infectious virus was present in any sample. A generalized estimating equations model was used to estimate how the probability of a positive result changed with the number of days since symptom onset. The sharpest decline occurred in saliva: its estimated probability of testing positive fell from 52.2% on day 1 to 0.7% by day 7. Blood positivity declined more gradually. Serum and plasma positivity rates were both above 85% on day 3 and were approximately 30% by day 7. Urine remained at a low positivity level throughout, and the number of days since symptom onset was not significantly associated with a positive urine result. These are modeled probabilities based on the study’s observed specimens, rather than measurements of infectious virus or proof that a person remained contagious for the same duration. The models also describe the study population and sampling schedule, so the day-specific estimates should not be interpreted as universal values for every patient or every specimen collection method. The relatively low number of positive urine samples further limited the precision of conclusions about that fluid. Parametric survival analysis provided additional estimates of the duration of detection. The median duration was 5.8 days in serum, with a 95% confidence interval of 4.8 to 6.9 days, and also 5.8 days in plasma, with a 95% confidence interval of 4.7 to 7.1 days. Saliva had a shorter median detection period of 3.5 days, with a 95% confidence interval of 3.0 to 4.1 days. Urine was excluded from this analysis because too few urine samples tested positive to support the model. Taken together, the results show that blood specimens retained detectable chikungunya virus longer and with greater consistency than the non-blood fluids examined. Saliva performed better than urine for detecting the virus during the acute phase, but its modeled positivity fell quickly. The findings support blood as the preferred sample type for detecting chikungunya virus and estimating how long detection persisted in the body during the period studied. They do not establish the duration of viable virus, whether transmission could occur from any specimen, or whether the same patterns occur outside hospitalized patients. The study was conducted in a single city during the 2025 outbreak, and its hospitalized population may not represent the wider range of chikungunya infections. Repeated specimens were available for 53 patients, but the analysis was limited to the body-fluid samples collected from that cohort and to the laboratory tests performed. Within those limits, the results provide a specimen-focused account of chikungunya detection dynamics during acute disease and identify differences between blood, saliva and urine that may help frame subsequent surveillance and public health control work.
